entries.efaa1760b673363a173ea05db29fd8b346d3d918: <div sID="gen24484" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Mark.5" sID="Mark.5"/> <div eID="gen24484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24485" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24486" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, we have, I. Christ's casting the legion of devils out of the man possessed, and suffering them to enter into the swine, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.1-Mark.5.20">ver. 1-20</reference>. II. Christ's healing the woman with the bloody issue, in the way as he was going to raise Jairus's daughter to life, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.21-Mark.5.43">ver. 21-43</reference>. These three miracles we had the story of before (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.28">Matt. viii. 28,</reference> and <reference osisRef="Matt.9.18">Matt. ix. 18</reference>, and c.) but more fully related here.
entries.7a2921fc8040c72c47451a39c55a637d57c51683: <div eID="gen24486" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24485" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Expulsion of Legion.</title> <div sID="gen24487" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And they came over unto the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes. <hi type="super">2</hi> And when he was come out of the ship, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit, <hi type="super">3</hi> Who had <hi type="italic">his</hi> dwelling among the tombs; and no man could bind him, no, not with chains: 4 Because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces: neither could any <hi type="italic">man</hi> tame him. 5 And always, night and day, he was in the mountains, and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones. <hi type="super">6</hi> But when he saw Jesus afar off, he ran and worshipped him, <hi type="super">7</hi> And cried with a loud voice, and said, What have I to do with thee, Jesus, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> Son of the most high God? I adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not. <hi type="super">8</hi> For he said unto him, Come out of the man, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> unclean spirit. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he asked him, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy name? And he answered, saying, My name <hi type="italic">is</hi> Legion: for we are many. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he besought him much that he would not send them away out of the country. <hi type="super">11</hi> Now there was there nigh unto the mountains a great herd of swine feeding. 12 And all the devils besought him, saying, Send us into the swine, that we may enter into them. <hi type="super">13</hi> And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea. 14 And they that fed the swine fled, and told <hi type="italic">it</hi> in the city, and in the country. And they went out to see what it was that was done. <hi type="super">15</hi> And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid. <hi type="super">16</hi> And they that saw <hi type="italic">it</hi> told them how it befell to him that was possessed with the devil, and <hi type="italic">also</hi> concerning the swine. 17 And they began to pray him to depart out of their coasts. 18 And when he was come into the ship, he that had been possessed with the devil prayed him that he might be with him. 19 Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee. <hi type="super">20</hi> And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all <hi type="italic">men</hi> did marvel. <div eID="gen24487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24488" type="x-p"/> We have here an instance of Christ's dispossessing the strong man armed, and disposing of him as he pleased, to make it appear that he was <hi type="italic">stronger than he.</hi> This he did when he was come <hi type="italic">to the other side,</hi> whither he went through a storm; his business there was to rescue this poor creature out of the hands of Satan, and when he had done that, he returned. Thus he came from heaven to earth, and returned, in a storm, to redeem a remnant of mankind out of the hands of the devil, though but a <hi type="italic">little remnant,</hi> and did not think his pains <hi type="italic">ill bestowed.</hi> <div eID="gen24488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24489" type="x-p"/> In Matthew, they were said to be <hi type="italic">two</hi> possessed with devils; here it is said to be a <hi type="italic">man</hi> possessed with an unclean spirit. If there were <hi type="italic">two,</hi> there was one, and Mark doth not say that there was <hi type="italic">but one;</hi> so that this difference cannot give us any just offence; it is probable that one of them was much more remarkable than the other, and said what was said. Now observe here, <div eID="gen24489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24490" type="x-p"/> I. The miserable condition that this poor creature was in; he was under the power of an <hi type="italic">unclean spirit,</hi> the devil got possession of him, and the effect of it was not, as in many, a silent melancholy, but a raging frenzy; he was raving mad; his condition seems to have been worse than any of the possessed, that were Christ's patients. <div eID="gen24490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24491" type="x-p"/> 1. He had <hi type="italic">his dwelling among the tombs,</hi> among the graves of dead people. Their tombs were out of the cities, in <hi type="italic">desolate places</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.3.14">Job iii. 14</reference>); which gave the devil great advantage: for <hi type="italic">woe to him that is alone.</hi> Perhaps the devil drove him to <hi type="italic">the tombs,</hi> to make people fancy that the souls of the dead were turned into dæmons, and did what mischief was done, so to excuse themselves from it. The touch of a grave was polluting, <reference osisRef="Num.19.16">Num. xix. 16</reference>. The <hi type="italic">unclean spirit</hi> drives people into that company that is <hi type="italic">defiling,</hi> and so keeps possession of them. Christ, by rescuing souls out of Satan's power, <hi type="italic">saves the living from among the dead.</hi> <div eID="gen24491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24492" type="x-p"/> 2. He was very strong and ungovernable; <hi type="italic">No man could bind him,</hi> as it is requisite both for their own good, and for the safety of others, that those who are distracted should be. Not only cords would not hold him, but <hi type="italic">chains</hi> and <hi type="italic">fetters of iron</hi> would not, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.3-Mark.5.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. Very deplorable is the case of such as <hi type="italic">need to be</hi> thus <hi type="italic">bound,</hi> and of all miserable people in this world they are most to be pitied; but his case was worst of all, in whom the devil was so strong, that he could not be <hi type="italic">bound.</hi> This sets forth the sad condition of those souls in which the devil has dominion; those <hi type="italic">children of disobedience,</hi> in whom that unclean spirit works. Some notoriously wilful sinners are like this madman; all are herein <hi type="italic">like the horse and the mule,</hi> that they need to be <hi type="italic">held in with bit and bridle;</hi> but some are like the <hi type="italic">wild ass,</hi> that will not be so held. The commands and curses of the law are as <hi type="italic">chains</hi> and <hi type="italic">fetters,</hi> to restrain sinners from their wicked courses; but they <hi type="italic">break those bands in sunder,</hi> and it is an evidence of the power of the devil in them. <div eID="gen24492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24493" type="x-p"/> 3. He was a terror and torment to himself and to all about him, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.5">v. 5</reference>. The devil is a <hi type="italic">cruel</hi> master to those that are <hi type="italic">led captive</hi> by him, a perfect tyrant; this wretched creature was <hi type="italic">night and day in the mountains and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones,</hi> either bemoaning his own deplorable case, or in a rage and indignation against heaven. Men in frenzies often wound and destroy themselves; what is a man, when reason is <hi type="italic">de</hi>throned and Satan <hi type="italic">en</hi>throned? The worshippers of Baal in their fury <hi type="italic">cut themselves,</hi> like this madman in his. The voice of God is, <hi type="italic">Do thyself no harm;</hi> the voice of Satan is, <hi type="italic">Do thyself all the harm thou canst;</hi> yet God's word is despised, and Satan's regarded. Perhaps his <hi type="italic">cutting himself with stones</hi> was only cutting his feet with the sharp stones he ran barefoot upon. <div eID="gen24493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24494" type="x-p"/> II. His application to Christ (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.6">v. 6</reference>); <hi type="italic">When he saw Jesus afar off,</hi> coming ashore, he <hi type="italic">ran, and worshipped him.</hi> He usually <hi type="italic">ran upon</hi> others with <hi type="italic">rage,</hi> but he <hi type="italic">ran to</hi> Christ with <hi type="italic">reverence.</hi> That was done by an invisible hand of Christ, which could not be done with chains and fetters; his fury was all on a sudden curbed. Even the devil, in this poor creature, was forced to tremble before Christ, and bow to him: or, rather, the poor man came, and <hi type="italic">worshipped Christ,</hi> in a sense of the need he had of his help, the power of Satan in and over him being, for this instant, suspended. <div eID="gen24494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24495" type="x-p"/> III. The word of command Christ gave to the unclean spirit, to quit his possession (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.8">v. 8</reference>); <hi type="italic">Come out of him, thou unclean spirit.</hi> He made the man desirous to be relieved, when he enabled him to <hi type="italic">run, and worship him,</hi> and then put forth his power for his relief. If Christ <hi type="italic">work in us</hi> heartily to pray for a deliverance from Satan, he will work for us that deliverance. Here is an instance of the power and authority with which Christ <hi type="italic">commanded the unclean spirits, and they obeyed him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.1.27">ch. i. 27</reference>. He said, <hi type="italic">Come out of the man.</hi> The design of Christ's gospel is to <hi type="italic">expel</hi> unclean spirits out of the souls of people; "<hi type="italic">Come out of the man, thou unclean spirit,</hi> that the Holy Spirit may enter, may take possession of the heart, and have dominion in it." <div eID="gen24495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24496" type="x-p"/> IV. The dread which the devil had of Christ. The <hi type="italic">man ran,</hi> and <hi type="italic">worshipped Christ;</hi> but it was the devil in the man, that <hi type="italic">cried with a loud voice</hi> (making use of the poor man's tongue), <hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.7">v. 7</reference>. Just as that other unclean spirit, <reference osisRef="Mark.1.24">ch. i. 24</reference>. 1. He calls God the <hi type="italic">most high God,</hi> above all other gods. By the name <hi type="italic">Elion—the Most High,</hi> God was <hi type="italic">known</hi> among the Ph&#339;nicians, and the other nations that bordered upon Israel; and by that name the devil calls him. 2. He owns Jesus to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God.</hi> Note, It is no strange thing to hear the best words drop from the worst mouths. There is such a way of saying this as none can attain to but <hi type="italic">by the Holy Ghost</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">1 Cor. xii. 3</reference>); yet it may be said, after a sort, by the <hi type="italic">unclean spirit.</hi> There is no judging of men by their loose sayings; but by their fruits ye shall know them. Piety from the teeth outward is an easy thing. The most fair-spoken hypocrite cannot say better than to call Jesus the Son of God, and yet that the devil did. 3. He disowns any design against Christ; "<hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> I have no need of thee, I pretend to none; I desire to have nothing to do with thee; I <hi type="italic">cannot stand</hi> before thee, and <hi type="italic">would not</hi> fall." 4. He deprecates his wrath; I <hi type="italic">adjure thee,</hi> that is, "I earnestly beseech thee, by all that is sacred, I beg of thee for God's sake, by whose permission I have got possession of this man, that, though thou drive me out hence, yet that thou <hi type="italic">torment me not,</hi> that thou do not restrain me from doing mischief somewhere else; though I know I am <hi type="italic">sentenced,</hi> yet let me not be <hi type="italic">sent</hi> to the chains of darkness, or hindered from going to and fro, to <hi type="italic">devour.</hi>" <div eID="gen24496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24497" type="x-p"/> V. The account Christ took from this unclean spirit of his name. This we had not in Matthew. Christ asked him, <hi type="italic">What is thy name?</hi> Not but that Christ could call all the <hi type="italic">fallen</hi> stars, as well as the <hi type="italic">morning</hi> stars, by their names; but he demands this, that the standers by might be affected with the vast numbers and power of those malignant infernal spirits, as they had reason to be, when the answer was, <hi type="italic">My name is Legion, for we are many;</hi> a <hi type="italic">legion</hi> of soldiers among the Romans consisted, some say, of six thousand men, others of twelve thousand and five hundred; but the number of a legion with them, like that of a regiment with us, was not always the same. Now this intimates that the devils, the infernal powers, are, 1. <hi type="italic">Military</hi> powers; a legion is a number of soldiers in arms. The devils war against God and his glory, Christ and his gospel, men and their holiness and happiness. They are such as we are to <hi type="italic">resist</hi> and <hi type="italic">wrestle against,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Eph. vi. 12</reference>. 2. That they are <hi type="italic">numerous;</hi> he <hi type="italic">owns,</hi> or rather he <hi type="italic">boasts—We are many;</hi> as if he hoped to be <hi type="italic">too many</hi> for Christ himself to deal with. What multitudes of apostate spirits were there, and all enemies to God and man; when here were a legion posted to keep garrison in one poor wretched creature against Christ! Many there are that rise up against us. 3. That they are <hi type="italic">unanimous;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">many</hi> devils, and yet but <hi type="italic">one legion</hi> engaged in the same wicked cause; and therefore that cavil of the Pharisees, which supposed Satan to cast out Satan, and to be divided against himself, was altogether groundless. It was not <hi type="italic">one</hi> of this legion that betrayed the rest, for they all said, as one man, <hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> 4. That they are very <hi type="italic">powerful;</hi> Who can stand before a <hi type="italic">legion?</hi> We are not a match for our spiritual enemies, in our own strength; but <hi type="italic">in the Lord, and in the power of his might,</hi> we shall be able to <hi type="italic">stand against them,</hi> though there are legions of them. 5. That there is <hi type="italic">order</hi> among them, as there is in a <hi type="italic">legion;</hi> there are <hi type="italic">principalities, and powers, and rulers of the darkness of this world,</hi> which supposes that there are those of a lower rank; the <hi type="italic">devil</hi> and his angels; the <hi type="italic">dragon</hi> and his; the prince of the devils and his subjects: which makes those enemies the more formidable. <div eID="gen24497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24498" type="x-p"/> VI. The request of this legion, that Christ would suffer them to go into a herd of swine that was <hi type="italic">feeding nigh unto the mountains</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.11">v. 11</reference>), those mountains which the demoniacs haunted, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.5">v. 5</reference>. Their request was, 1. That he <hi type="italic">would not send them away out of the country</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.10">v. 10</reference>); not only that he would not <hi type="italic">commit</hi> them, or <hi type="italic">confine</hi> them, to their infernal prison, and so <hi type="italic">torment them before the time;</hi> but that he would not <hi type="italic">banish</hi> them <hi type="italic">that country,</hi> as justly he might, because in this poor man they had been such a terror to it, and done so much mischief. They seem to have had a particular affection for <hi type="italic">that country;</hi> or, rather, a particular spite to it; and to have liberty to walk <hi type="italic">to and fro through</hi> the rest of <hi type="italic">the earth,</hi> will not serve (<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job i. 7</reference>), unless the <hi type="italic">range of those mountains</hi> be allowed them for their pasture, <reference osisRef="Job.39.8">Job xxxix. 8</reference>. But why would they abide in <hi type="italic">that country?</hi> Grotius saith, Because in <hi type="italic">that country</hi> there were many <hi type="italic">apostate Jews,</hi> who had thrown themselves out of the covenant of God, and had thereby given Satan power over them. And some suggest, that, having by experience got the knowledge of the dispositions and manners of the people of that country, they could the more effectually do them mischief by their temptations. 2. That he would suffer them to <hi type="italic">enter into the swine,</hi> by destroying which they hoped to do more mischief to the souls of all the people in the country, than they could by entering into the body of any particular person, which therefore they did not ask leave to do, for they knew Christ would not grant it. <div eID="gen24498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24499" type="x-p"/> VII. The permission Christ gave them to enter into the swine, and the immediate destruction of the swine thereby; <hi type="italic">He gave them leave</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.13">v. 13</reference>), he did not forbid or restrain them, he let them do as they had a mind. Thus he would let the Gadarenes see what powerful spiteful enemies devils are, that they might thereby be induced to make him their Friend, who alone was able to control and conquer them, and had made it appear that he was so. Immediately the <hi type="italic">unclean spirits entered into the swine,</hi> which by the law were unclean creatures, and naturally love to <hi type="italic">wallow in the mire,</hi> the fittest place for them. Those that, like the swine, delight in <hi type="italic">the mire</hi> of sensual lusts, are fit habitations for Satan, and are, like Babylon, the <hi type="italic">hold of every foul spirit,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">cage of every unclean and hateful bird</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Rev. xviii. 2</reference>), as pure souls are habitations of the Holy Spirit. The consequence of the devils entering into the swine, was, that they all <hi type="italic">ran mad</hi> presently, and ran headlong into the adjoining sea, where they were all drowned, to the number of <hi type="italic">two thousand.</hi> The man they possessed did only <hi type="italic">cut himself,</hi> for God had said, <hi type="italic">He is in your hands, only save his life.</hi> But thereby it appeared, that, if he had not been so restrained, the poor man would have <hi type="italic">drowned himself.</hi> See how much we are indebted to the providence of God, and the ministration of good angels, for our preservation from malignant spirits. <div eID="gen24499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24500" type="x-p"/> VIII. The report of all this dispersed through the country immediately. They that <hi type="italic">fed the swine,</hi> hastened to the owners, to give an account of their charge, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.14">v. 14</reference>. This drew the people together, to see what was done: and, 1. When they saw how wonderfully the poor man was cured, they hence conceived a <hi type="italic">veneration for Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.15">v. 15</reference>. They saw him that was <hi type="italic">possessed with the devil,</hi> and knew him well enough, by the same token that they had many a time been frightened at the sight of him; and were now as much surprised to see him <hi type="italic">sitting clothed and in his right mind;</hi> when Satan was cast out, he came to himself, and was his own man presently. Note, Those who are grave and sober, and live by rule and with consideration, thereby make it appear that by the power of Christ the devil's power is broken in their souls. The sight of this <hi type="italic">made them afraid;</hi> it astonished them, and forced them to own the power of Christ, and that he is <hi type="italic">worthy to be feared.</hi> But, 2. When they found that their swine were lost, they thence conceived a <hi type="italic">dislike of Christ,</hi> and wished to have rather his room than his company; they prayed him to <hi type="italic">depart out of their coasts,</hi> for they think not any good he can do them sufficient to make them amends for the loss of so many swine, fat swine, it may be, and ready for the market. Now the devils had what they would have; for by no handle do these evil spirits more effectually manage sinful souls than by that of the love of the world. They were afraid of some further punishment, if Christ should tarry among them, whereas, if they would but part with their sins, he had life and happiness for them; but, being loth to quit either their sins or their swine, they chose rather to abandon their Saviour. Thus <hi type="italic">they</hi> do, who, rather than let go a base lust, will throw away their interest in Christ, and their expectations from him. They should rather have argued, "If he has such a power as this over devils and all creatures, it is good having him our Friend; if the devils have leave to tarry <hi type="italic">in our country</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.10">v. 10</reference>), let us entreat <hi type="italic">him</hi> to tarry in it too, who alone can control them." But, instead of this, they wished him further off. Such strange misconstructions do carnal hearts make of the just judgments of God; instead of being by them driven to him as they ought, they set him at so much the greater distance; though he hath said, <hi type="italic">Provoke me not, and I will do you no hurt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.25.6">Jer. xxv. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen24500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24501" type="x-p"/> IX. An account of the conduct of the poor man after his deliverance. 1. He <hi type="italic">desired that he might go along with Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.18">v. 18</reference>), perhaps for fear lest the evil spirit should again seize him; or, rather, that he might receive instruction from him, being unwilling to stay among those heathenish people that desired him to depart. Those that are freed from the evil spirit, cannot but covet acquaintance and fellowship with Christ. 2. Christ <hi type="italic">would not suffer him</hi> to go with him, lest it should savour of ostentation, and to let him know that he could both protect and instruct him at a distance. And besides, he had other work for him to do; he must go home to his friends, and tell them what <hi type="italic">great things the Lord had done for him,</hi> the Lord Jesus had done; that Christ might be honoured, and his neighbours and friends might be edified, and invited to believe in Christ. He must take particular notice rather of Christ's <hi type="italic">pity</hi> than of his <hi type="italic">power,</hi> for that is it which especially he glories in; he must tell them what <hi type="italic">compassion</hi> the Lord had had on him in his misery. 3. The man, in a transport of joy, proclaimed, all the country over, what <hi type="italic">great things Jesus had done for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.20">v. 20</reference>. This is a debt we owe both to Christ and to our brethren, that he may be glorified and they edified. And see what was the effect of it; <hi type="italic">All men did marvel,</hi> but few went any further. Many that cannot but wonder at the works of Christ, yet do not, as they ought, <hi type="italic">wonder after him.</hi>
entries.abe52c75730f0a48a67e610f34c25d275935b52a: <div eID="gen24501" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Healing of the Bloody Issue.</title> <div sID="gen24502" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> And when Jesus was passed over again by ship unto the other side, much people gathered unto him: and he was nigh unto the sea. <hi type="super">22</hi> And, behold, there cometh one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name; and when he saw him, he fell at his feet, <hi type="super">23</hi> And besought him greatly, saying, My little daughter lieth at the point of death: <hi type="italic">I pray thee,</hi> come and lay thy hands on her, that she may be healed; and she shall live. 24 And <hi type="italic">Jesus</hi> went with him; and much people followed him, and thronged him. <hi type="super">25</hi> And a certain woman, which had an issue of blood twelve years, <hi type="super">26</hi> And had suffered many things of many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse, <hi type="super">27</hi> When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment. <hi type="super">28</hi> For she said, If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole. 29 And straightway the fountain of her blood was dried up; and she felt in <hi type="italic">her</hi> body that she was healed of that plague. 30 And Jesus, immediately knowing in himself that virtue had gone out of him, turned him about in the press, and said, Who touched my clothes? <hi type="super">31</hi> And his disciples said unto him, Thou seest the multitude thronging thee, and sayest thou, Who touched me? <hi type="super">32</hi> And he looked round about to see her that had done this thing. <hi type="super">33</hi> But the woman fearing and trembling, knowing what was done in her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth. <hi type="super">34</hi> And he said unto her, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague. <div eID="gen24502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24503" type="x-p"/> The Gadarenes having desired Christ to leave their country, he did not stay to trouble them long, but presently went by water, as he came, back <hi type="italic">to the other side</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.21">v. 21</reference>), and there <hi type="italic">much people gathered to him.</hi> Note, If there be some that reject Christ, yet there are others that receive him, and bid him welcome. A despised gospel will <hi type="italic">cross the water,</hi> and go where it will have better entertainment. Now among the many that applied themselves to him, <div eID="gen24503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24504" type="x-p"/> I. Here is one, that comes <hi type="italic">openly</hi> to <hi type="italic">beg</hi> a cure for a sick child; and it is no less a person than one of the <hi type="italic">rulers of the synagogue,</hi> one that presided in the synagogue-worship or, as some think, one of the judges of the consistory court, which was in every city, consisting of <hi type="italic">twenty-three.</hi> He was not named in Matthew, he is here, <hi type="italic">Jairus,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Jair,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.10.3">Judg. x. 3</reference>. He addressed himself to Christ, though a ruler, with great humility and reverence; <hi type="italic">When he saw him, he fell at his feet,</hi> giving honour to him as one really greater than he appeared to be; and with great importunity, he <hi type="italic">besought him greatly,</hi> as one in earnest, as one that not only valued the mercy he came for, but that knew he could obtain it no where else. The case is this, He has a <hi type="italic">little daughter,</hi> about twelve years old, the darling of the family, and she <hi type="italic">lies a dying;</hi> but he believes that if Christ will but come, and <hi type="italic">lay his hands upon her,</hi> she will return even from the gates of the grave. He said, at first, when he came, <hi type="italic">She lies a dying</hi> (so Mark); but afterward, upon fresh information sent him, he saith, <hi type="italic">She is even now dead</hi> (so Matthew); but he still prosecutes his suit; see <reference osisRef="Luke.8.42-Luke.8.49">Luke viii. 42-49</reference>. Christ readily agreed, and went with him, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.24">v. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen24504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24505" type="x-p"/> II. Here is another, that comes <hi type="italic">clandestinely</hi> to <hi type="italic">steal</hi> a cure (if I may so say) for herself; and she got the relief she came for. This cure was wrought by <hi type="italic">the way,</hi> as he was going to raise the ruler's daughter, and was followed by a crowd. See how Christ improved his time, and lost none of the precious moments of it. Many of his discourses, and some of his miracles, are dates <hi type="italic">by the way-side;</hi> we should be doing good, not only when we <hi type="italic">sit in the house,</hi> but when we <hi type="italic">walk by the way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.6.7">Deut. vi. 7</reference>. Now observe, <div eID="gen24505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24506" type="x-p"/> 1. The piteous case of this poor woman. She had a constant <hi type="italic">issue of blood</hi> upon her, for <hi type="italic">twelve years,</hi> which had thrown her, no doubt, into great weakness, had embittered the comfort of her life, and threatened to be her death in a little time. She had had the best advice of physicians, that she could get, and had made use of the many medicines and methods they prescribed: as long as she had any thing to give them, they had kept her in hopes that they could cure her; but now that she had spent all she had among them, they gave her up as incurable. See here, (1.) That skin for skin, and all that a man has, will be give for life and health; she spent all she had upon physicians. (2.) It is ill with those patients whose physicians are their worst disease; who <hi type="italic">suffer</hi> by their physicians, instead of being relieved by them. (3.) Those that are not <hi type="italic">bettered</hi> by medicines, commonly <hi type="italic">grow worse,</hi> and the disease gets the more ground. (4.) It is usual with people not to apply themselves to Christ, till they have tried in vain all other helpers, and find them, as certainly they will, <hi type="italic">physicians of no value.</hi> And he will be found a <hi type="italic">sure refuge,</hi> even to those who make him their <hi type="italic">last refuge.</hi> <div eID="gen24506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24507" type="x-p"/> 2. The strong faith that she had in the power of Christ to heal her; she said within herself, though it doth not appear that she was encouraged by any preceding instance to say it, <hi type="italic">If I may but touch his clothes, I shall be whole,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.28">v. 28</reference>. She believed that he cured, not as a prophet, by virtue <hi type="italic">derived</hi> from God, but as the Son of God, by a virtue <hi type="italic">inherent</hi> in himself. Her case was such as she could not in modesty tell him publicly, as others did their grievances, and therefore a private cure was what she wished for, and her faith was suited to her case. <div eID="gen24507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24508" type="x-p"/> 3. The wonderful effect produced by it; <hi type="italic">She came in the</hi> crowd <hi type="italic">behind</hi> him, and with much ado got to <hi type="italic">touch his garment,</hi> and immediately she felt the cure wrought, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.29">v. 29</reference>. The flux of blood was <hi type="italic">dried up,</hi> and she felt herself perfectly well all over her, as well as ever she was in her life, in an instant; by this it appears that the cure was altogether miraculous; for those that in such cases are cured by natural means, recover their strength slowly and gradually, and not <hi type="italic">per saltum—all at once;</hi> but <hi type="italic">as for God, his work is perfect.</hi> Note, Those whom Christ heals of the disease of sin, that bloody issue, cannot but experience in themselves a universal change for the better. <div eID="gen24508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24509" type="x-p"/> 4. Christ's enquiry after his concealed patient, and the encouragement he gave her, upon the discovery of her; Christ <hi type="italic">knew in himself that virtue had gone out of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.30">v. 30</reference>. He knew it not by any deficiency of spirits, through the exhausting of this virtue, but rather by an agility of spirits, in the exerting of it, and the innate and inseparable pleasure he had in doing good. And being desirous to see his patient, he asked, not in displeasure, as one affronted, but in tenderness, as one concerned, <hi type="italic">Who touched my clothes?</hi> The disciples, not without a show of rudeness and indecency, almost ridiculed his question (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.31">v. 31</reference>); <hi type="italic">The multitudes throng thee, and sayest thou, Who touched me?</hi> As if it had been an improper question. Christ passed by the affront, and <hi type="italic">looks around</hi> to <hi type="italic">see her that had done this thing;</hi> not that he might <hi type="italic">blame</hi> her for her presumption, but that he might <hi type="italic">commend</hi> and <hi type="italic">encourage</hi> her faith, and by his own act and deed might <hi type="italic">warrant</hi> and <hi type="italic">confirm</hi> the cure, and <hi type="italic">ratify</hi> to her that which she had <hi type="italic">surreptitiously</hi> obtained. He needed not that any should inform him, for he had presently his eye upon her. Note, As secret acts of sin, so secret acts of faith, are known to the Lord Jesus, and are under his eye. If believers derive virtue from Christ ever so closely, he knows it, and is pleased with it. The poor woman, hereupon, presented herself to the Lord Jesus (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.33">v. 33</reference>), <hi type="italic">fearing and trembling,</hi> not knowing how he would take it. Note, Christ's patients are often trembling, when they have reason to be triumphing. She might have come boldly, <hi type="italic">knowing what was done in her;</hi> yet, <hi type="italic">knowing that,</hi> she <hi type="italic">fears</hi> and <hi type="italic">trembles.</hi> It was a <hi type="italic">surprise,</hi> and was not yet, as it should have been, a <hi type="italic">pleasing</hi> surprise. However, she <hi type="italic">fell down before him.</hi> Note, There is nothing better for those that fear and tremble, than to throw themselves at the feet of the Lord Jesus; to humble themselves before him, and refer themselves to him. And she <hi type="italic">told him all the truth.</hi> Note, We must not be ashamed to own the secret transactions between Christ and our souls; but, when called to it, mention, to his praise, and the encouragement of others, what he has done for our souls, and the experience we have had of <hi type="italic">healing virtue</hi> derived from him. And the consideration of this, that nothing can be hid from Christ, should engage us to confess all to him. See what an encouraging word he gave her (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.34">v. 34</reference>); <hi type="italic">Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole.</hi> Note, Christ puts honour upon faith, because faith gives honour to Christ. But see how <hi type="italic">what is done by faith</hi> on earth is ratified in heaven; Christ saith, <hi type="italic">Be whole of thy disease.</hi> Note, If our faith sets the seal of its <hi type="italic">amen</hi> to the power and promise of God, saying, "So it is, and so let it be to me;" God's grace will set the seal of its <hi type="italic">amen</hi> to the prayers and hopes of faith, saying, "So be it, and so it shall be, to thee." And therefore, "<hi type="italic">Go in peace;</hi> be well satisfied that thy cure is honestly come by, is effectually wrought, and take the comfort of it." Note, They that by faith are healed of their spiritual diseases, have reason to <hi type="italic">go in peace.</hi>
entries.b51d79b669b76ea6632a81e83ae7bcc7d384325a: <div eID="gen24509" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Daughter of Jairus Restored to Life.</title> <div sID="gen24510" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> While he yet spake, there came from the ruler of the synagogue's <hi type="italic">house certain</hi> which said, Thy daughter is dead: why troublest thou the Master any further? <hi type="super">36</hi> As soon as Jesus heard the word that was spoken, he saith unto the ruler of the synagogue, Be not afraid, only believe. <hi type="super">37</hi> And he suffered no man to follow him, save Peter, and James, and John the brother of <reference osisRef="Jas.38">James. 38</reference> And he cometh to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and seeth the tumult, and them that wept and wailed greatly. <hi type="super">39</hi> And when he was come in, he saith unto them, Why make ye this ado, and weep? the damsel is not dead, but sleepeth. <hi type="super">40</hi> And they laughed him to scorn. But when he had put them all out, he taketh the father and the mother of the damsel, and them that were with him, and entereth in where the damsel was lying. <hi type="super">41</hi> And he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise. <hi type="super">42</hi> And straightway the damsel arose, and walked; for she was <hi type="italic">of the age</hi> of twelve years. And they were astonished with a great astonishment. <hi type="super">43</hi> And he charged them straitly that no man should know it; and commanded that something should be given her to eat. <div eID="gen24510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24511" type="x-p"/> Diseases and deaths came into the world by the sin and disobedience of the first Adam; but by the grace of the second Adam both are conquered. Christ, having healed an incurable disease, here goes on to triumph over death, as in the beginning of the chapter he had triumphed over an outrageous devil. <div eID="gen24511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24512" type="x-p"/> I. The melancholy news is brought to Jairus, that his <hi type="italic">daughter is dead,</hi> and therefore, if Christ be as other physicians, he comes too late. While there is life, there is hope, and room for the use of means; but when life is gone, it is past recall; <hi type="italic">Why troublest thou the Master any further?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.35">v. 35</reference>. Ordinarily, the proper thought in this case, is, "The matter is determined, the will of God is done, and I submit, I acquiesce; <hi type="italic">The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away. While the child was alive, I fasted and wept; for I said, Who can tell but God will yet be gracious to me,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the child shall live?</hi> But <hi type="italic">now that it is dead, wherefore should I weep?</hi> I <hi type="italic">shall go to it, but it shall not return to me.</hi>" With such words we should <hi type="italic">quiet ourselves</hi> at such a time, that our souls may be <hi type="italic">as a child that is weaned from his mother:</hi> but there the case was extraordinary; the death of the child doth not, as usually, put an end to the narrative. <div eID="gen24512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24513" type="x-p"/> II. Christ encourageth the afflicted father yet to hope that his application to Christ on the behalf of his child should not be in vain. Christ had staid to work a cure by the way, but he shall be no sufferer by that, nor loser by the gain of others; <hi type="italic">Be not afraid, only believe.</hi> We may suppose Jairus at a pause, whether he should ask Christ to go on or no; but have we not as much occasion for the grace of God, and his consolations, and consequently of the prayers of our ministers and Christian friends, when death is in the house, as when sickness is? Christ therefore soon determines this matter; "<hi type="italic">Be not afraid</hi> that my coming will be to no purpose, only believe that I will make it turn to a good account." Note, 1. We must not despair concerning our relations that are dead, nor <hi type="italic">sorrow</hi> for them <hi type="italic">as those that have no hope.</hi> See what is said to Rachel, who <hi type="italic">refused to be comforted concerning her children,</hi> upon the presumption that they <hi type="italic">were not; Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears; for there is hope in thine end, that thy children shall come again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.31.16-Jer.31.17">Jer. xxxi. 16, 17</reference>. Therefore fear not, faint not. 2. Faith is the only remedy against disquieting grief and fear at such a time: let that silence them, <hi type="italic">Only believe.</hi> Keep up a confidence in Christ, and a dependence upon him, and he will do what is for the best. Believe the resurrection, and then be not afraid. <div eID="gen24513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24514" type="x-p"/> III. He went with a select company to the house where the dead child was. He had, by the crowd that attended him, given advantage to the poor woman he last healed, and, having done that, now he shook off the crowd, and <hi type="italic">suffered no man to follow him</hi> (to <hi type="italic">follow with him,</hi> so the word is), but his three bosom-disciples, Peter, and James, and John; a competent number to be witnesses of the miracle, but not such a number as that his taking them with him might look like vainglory. <div eID="gen24514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24515" type="x-p"/> IV. He raised the dead child to life; the circumstances of the narrative here are much the same as we had them in Matthew; only here we may observe, <div eID="gen24515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24516" type="x-p"/> 1. That the child was extremely well beloved, for the relations and neighbours <hi type="italic">wept and wailed greatly.</hi> It is very afflictive when that which is come forth like a flower is so <hi type="italic">soon cut down,</hi> and withereth before it is grown up; when that grieves us, of which we said, <hi type="italic">This same shall comfort us.</hi> <div eID="gen24516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24517" type="x-p"/> 2. That it was evident beyond dispute, that the child was really and truly dead. Their <hi type="italic">laughing</hi> Christ to <hi type="italic">scorn,</hi> for saying, <hi type="italic">She is not dead, but sleepeth,</hi> though highly reprehensible, serves for the proof of this. <div eID="gen24517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24518" type="x-p"/> 3. That Christ put those out as unworthy to be witnesses of the miracle, who were noisy in their sorrow, and were so ignorant in the things of God, as not to understand him when he spoke of death as a <hi type="italic">sleep,</hi> or so scornful, as to ridicule him for it. <div eID="gen24518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24519" type="x-p"/> 4. That he took the parents of the child to be witnesses of the miracle, because in it he had an eye to <hi type="italic">their faith,</hi> and designed it for <hi type="italic">their</hi> comfort, who were the <hi type="italic">true,</hi> for they were the <hi type="italic">silent</hi> mourners. <div eID="gen24519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24520" type="x-p"/> 5. That Christ raised the child to life by a word of power, which is recorded here, and recorded in Syriac, the language in which Christ spoke, for the greater certainty of the thing; <hi type="italic">Talitha, cumi; Damsel, I say unto thee, Arise.</hi> Dr. Lightfoot saith, It was customary with the Jews, when they gave physic to one that was <hi type="italic">sick,</hi> to say, <hi type="italic">Arise from thy disease;</hi> meaning, <hi type="italic">We wish</hi> thou mayest arise: but to one that was <hi type="italic">dead,</hi> Christ said, <hi type="italic">Arise from the dead;</hi> meaning, <hi type="italic">I command</hi> that thou arise; nay, there is more in it—the dead have not power to arise, therefore power goes along with this word, to make it effectual. <hi type="italic">Da quod jubes, et jube quod vis—Give what thou commandest, and command what thou wilt.</hi> Christ works while he commands, and works by the command, and therefore may command what he pleaseth, even the dead to arise. Such is the gospel call to those that are by nature dead in trespasses and sins, and can no more rise from that death by their own power, than this child could; and yet that word, <hi type="italic">Awake, and arise from the dead,</hi> is neither vain, nor in vain, when it follows immediately, <hi type="italic">Christ shall give thee light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Eph. v. 14</reference>. It is by the word of Christ that spiritual life is given, <hi type="italic">I said unto thee, Live,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.6">Ezek. xvi. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen24520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24521" type="x-p"/> 6. That the damsel, as soon as life returned, <hi type="italic">arose, and walked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.42">v. 42</reference>. Spiritual life will appear by our <hi type="italic">rising</hi> from the bed of sloth and carelessness, and our <hi type="italic">walking</hi> in a religious conversation, our walking <hi type="italic">up and down</hi> in Christ's name and strength; even from those that are <hi type="italic">of the age of twelve years,</hi> it may be expected that they should walk as those whom Christ has <hi type="italic">raised to life,</hi> otherwise than in the native <hi type="italic">vanity of their minds.</hi> <div eID="gen24521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24522" type="x-p"/> 7. That all who saw it, and heard of it, admired the miracle, and him that wrought it; <hi type="italic">They were astonished with a great astonishment.</hi> They could not but acknowledge that there was something in it extraordinary and very great, and yet they knew not what to make of it, or to infer from it. Their wonder should have worked forward to a lively faith, but it rested in a <hi type="italic">stupor</hi> or <hi type="italic">astonishment.</hi> <div eID="gen24522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24523" type="x-p"/> 8. That Christ endeavoured to conceal it; <hi type="italic">He charged them straitly, that no man should know it.</hi> It was sufficiently known to a competent number, but he would not have it as yet <hi type="italic">proclaimed</hi> any further; because his own resurrection was to be the great instance of his power over death, and therefore the divulging of other instances must be reserved till that great proof was given: let one part of the evidence be kept private, till the other part, on which the main stress lies, be made ready. <div eID="gen24523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24524" type="x-p"/> 9. That Christ took care something should be <hi type="italic">given her to eat.</hi> By this it appeared that she was raised not only to life, but to a good state of health, that she had an appetite to her meat; even the new-born babes in Christ's house desire the sincere milk, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.1-1Pet.2.2">1 Pet. ii. 1, 2</reference>. And it is observable, that, as Christ, when at first he had made man, presently provided food for him, and food out of the earth of which he was made (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.29">Gen. i. 29</reference>), so now when he had given a new life, he took care that something should be given to eat; for is he has given <hi type="italic">life,</hi> he may be trusted to give <hi type="italic">livelihood,</hi> because <hi type="italic">the life is more than meat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.25">Matt. vi. 25</reference>. Where Christ hath given <hi type="italic">spiritual life,</hi> he will provide food for the support and nourishment of it unto life eternal, for he will <hi type="italic">never forsake,</hi> or be wanting to, the <hi type="italic">work of his own hands.</hi>  <chapter eID="Mark.5"/> <div eID="gen24524" type="x-p"/>

entries.ee9fa72fffad8a2e7e24679eb356a65ff66d4c79: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13922"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <div sID="gen26798" type="x-p"/> Glorious Cure of the Gadarene Demoniac (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.1-Mark.5.20">Mr 5:1-20</reference>).<div eID="gen26798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26799" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13922"/>1. And they came over unto the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes. <div eID="gen26799" type="x-p"/>
entries.e845384ff42277cd743ad671f7023814695b7188: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13923"/><div sID="gen26800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13923"/><hi type="bold">2. And when he was come out of the ship, immediately--</hi>(see <reference osisRef="Mark.5.6">Mr 5:6</reference>).<div eID="gen26800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there met him a man with an unclean spirit--</hi>"which had devils [demons] <hi type="bold">long time" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.27">Lu 8:27</reference>). In Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.28">Mt 8:28</reference>), "there met him two men possessed with devils." Though there be no discrepancy between these two statements--</hi>more than between two witnesses, one of whom testifies to something done by one person, while the other affirms that there were two--it is difficult to see how the principal details here given could apply to more than one case. <div eID="gen26801" type="x-p"/>
entries.076cb2f74f99e2630492955ec466dc9d09c36c0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13924"/><div sID="gen26802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13924"/><hi type="bold">3. Who had his dwelling among the tombs--</hi>Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.27">Lu 8:27</reference>) says, "He ware no clothes, neither abode in any house." These tombs were hewn out of the rocky caves of the locality, and served for shelters and lurking places (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.26">Lu 8:26</reference>). <div eID="gen26802" type="x-p"/>
entries.ada2bad809103b0d7500808f5117c4ee1483b8dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13925"/><div sID="gen26803" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13925"/><hi type="bold">4. Because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains, &c.--</hi>Luke says (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.29">Lu 8:29</reference>) that "oftentimes it [the unclean spirit] had caught him"; and after mentioning how they had vainly tried to bind him with chains and fetters, because, "he brake the bands," he adds, "and was driven of the devil [demon] into the wilderness." The dark tyrant-power by which he was held clothed him with superhuman strength and made him scorn restraint. Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.28">Mt 8:28</reference>) says he was "exceeding fierce, so that no man might pass by that way." He was the terror of the whole locality. <div eID="gen26803" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d61bef630437ca4ff40dc6e3ce0cd6a6ebb204b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13926"/><div sID="gen26804" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13926"/><hi type="bold">5. And always, night and day, he was in the mountains, and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones--</hi>Terrible as he was to others, he himself endured untold misery, which sought relief in tears and self-inflicted torture. <div eID="gen26804" type="x-p"/>
entries.7eeb99ce1dfe91f677d89060ff51f142d88a71ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13927"/><div sID="gen26805" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13927"/><hi type="bold">6. But when he saw Jesus afar off, he ran and worshipped him--</hi>not with the spontaneous alacrity which says to Jesus, "Draw me, we will run after thee," but inwardly compelled, with terrific rapidity, before the Judge, to receive sentence of expulsion. <div eID="gen26805" type="x-p"/>
entries.72ac40b0955f3e2c21aaf223bed7c0b5bdb8bbeb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13928"/><div sID="gen26806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13928"/>7. What have I to do with thee, Jesus, Son of the most high God? I <hi type="bold">adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not--</hi>or, as in <reference osisRef="Matt.8.29">Mt 8:29</reference>, "Art Thou come to torment us before the time?" (See on <reference osisRef="Mark.1.24">Mr 1:24</reference>). Behold the tormentor anticipating, dreading, and entreating exemption from torment! In Christ they discern their destined Tormentor; the time, they know, is fixed, and they feel as if it were come already! (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.19">Jas 2:19</reference>). <div eID="gen26806" type="x-p"/>
entries.29afb169a62de30ab37b71747dc28a91bc4fd1f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13929"/><div sID="gen26807" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13929"/><hi type="bold">8. For he said unto him--</hi>that is, before the unclean spirit cried out.<div eID="gen26807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Come out of the man, unclean spirit!--</hi>Ordinarily, obedience to a command of this nature was immediate. But here, a certain delay is permitted, the more signally to manifest the power of Christ and accomplish His purposes. <div eID="gen26808" type="x-p"/>
entries.bcd0b79dac98df44b912ba8c85575f816badcd35: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13930"/><div sID="gen26809" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13930"/><hi type="bold">9. And he asked him, What is thy name?--</hi>The object of this question was to extort an acknowledgment of the virulence of demoniacal power by which this victim was enthralled.<div eID="gen26809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And he answered, saying, My name is Legion: for we are many--</hi>or, as in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.30">Lu 8:30</reference>) "because many devils [demons] were entered into him." A <hi type="bold">legion, in the Roman army, amounted, at its full complement, to six thousand; but here the word is used, as such words with us, and even this one, for an indefinitely large number--</hi>large enough however to rush, as soon as permission was given, into two thousand swine and destroy them. <div eID="gen26810" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3ea3cd6d88a352f60120a37695b23085f9c7645: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13931"/><div sID="gen26811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13931"/><hi type="bold">10. And he besought him much that he would not send them away out of the country--</hi>The entreaty, it will be observed, was made by one spirit, but in behalf of many--"he besought Him not to send them, &c."--just as in <reference osisRef="Mark.5.9">Mr 5:9</reference>, "he answered we are many." But what do they mean by entreating so earnestly not to be ordered out of the country? Their next petition (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.12">Mr 5:12</reference>) will make that clear enough. <div eID="gen26811" type="x-p"/>
entries.07971836adc74b1fb6090bcc68e1c2000ab296a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13932"/><div sID="gen26812" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13932"/><hi type="bold">11. Now there was there, nigh unto the mountains--</hi>rather, "to the mountain," according to what is clearly the true reading. In <reference osisRef="Matt.8.30">Mt 8:30</reference>, they are said to have been "a good way off." But these expressions, far from being inconsistent, only confirm, by their precision, the minute accuracy of the narrative.<div eID="gen26812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a great herd of swine feeding--</hi>There can hardly be any doubt that the owners of these were Jews, since to them our Lord had now come to proffer His services. This will explain what follows. <div eID="gen26813" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4870292b65b9f519a47a7b165e1fae4bb175d2a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13933"/><div sID="gen26814" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13933"/><hi type="bold">12. And all the devils besought him, saying--</hi>"if thou cast us out" (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.31">Mt 8:31</reference>).<div eID="gen26814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Send us into the swine, that we may enter into them--</hi>Had they spoken out all their mind, perhaps this would have been it: "If we must quit our hold of this man, suffer us to continue our work of mischief in another form, that by entering these swine, and thus destroying the people's property, we may steel their hearts against Thee!" <div eID="gen26815" type="x-p"/>
entries.514d4484e2cfe4f891054d1e3b406481e5a8345a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13934"/><div sID="gen26816" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13934"/><hi type="bold">13. And forthwith Jesus gave them leave--</hi>In Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.32">Mt 8:32</reference>) this is given with majestic brevity--"Go!" The owners, if Jews, drove an illegal trade; if heathens, they insulted the national religion: in either case the permission was just.<div eID="gen26816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And the unclean spirits went out--</hi>of the man.<div eID="gen26817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently--</hi>rushed.<div eID="gen26818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26819" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">down a steep place--</hi>down the hanging cliff.<div eID="gen26819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into the sea (they were about two thousand)--</hi>The number of them is given by this graphic Evangelist alone.<div eID="gen26820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and were choked in the sea--</hi>"perished in the waters" (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.32">Mt 8:32</reference>). <div eID="gen26821" type="x-p"/>
entries.59c525e14f443b441911d76b3b2081716d226123: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13935"/><div sID="gen26822" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13935"/><hi type="bold">14. And they that fed the swine fled, and told it--</hi>"told everything, and what was befallen to the possessed of the devils" (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.33">Mt 8:33</reference>).<div eID="gen26822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26823" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the city, and in the country. And they went out to see what it was that was done--</hi>Thus had they the evidence, both of the herdsmen and of their own senses, to the reality of both miracles. <div eID="gen26823" type="x-p"/>
entries.3266fd3adbf2621658630144f37fb3360221d82f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13936"/><div sID="gen26824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13936"/><hi type="bold">15. And they come to Jesus--</hi>Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.34">Mt 8:34</reference>) says, "Behold, the whole city came out to meet Jesus."<div eID="gen26824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and see him that was possessed with the devil--</hi>the demonized person.<div eID="gen26825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and had the legion, sitting--</hi>"at the feet of Jesus," adds Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.35">Lu 8:35</reference>); in contrast with his former wild and wandering habits.<div eID="gen26826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26827" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and clothed--</hi>As our Evangelist had not told us that he "ware no clothes," the meaning of this statement could only have been conjectured but for "the beloved physician" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.27">Lu 8:27</reference>), who supplies the missing piece of information here. This is a striking case of what are called Undesigned Coincidences amongst the different Evangelists; one of them taking a thing for granted, as familiarly known at the time, but which we should never have known but for one or more of the others, and without the knowledge of which some of their statements would be unintelligible. The clothing which the poor man would feel the want of the moment his consciousness returned to him, was doubtless supplied to him by some of the Twelve.<div eID="gen26827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and in his right mind--</hi>but now, oh, in what a lofty sense! (Compare an analogous, though a different kind of case, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.34-Dan.4.37">Da 4:34-37</reference>).<div eID="gen26828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26829" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and they were afraid--</hi>Had this been awe only, it had been natural enough; but other feelings, alas! of a darker kind, soon showed themselves. <div eID="gen26829" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c97b290824e0659ce7f86933db1ba10fa8eec9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13937"/><div sID="gen26830" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13937"/><hi type="bold">16. And they that saw it told them how it befell to him that was possessed with the devil--</hi>("the demonized person").<div eID="gen26830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and also concerning the swine--</hi>Thus had they the double testimony of the herdsmen and their own senses. <div eID="gen26831" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2f3780c76b74ce2e9e098a7ad0bf1843f69b56a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13938"/><div sID="gen26832" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13938"/><hi type="bold">17. And they began to pray him to depart out of their coasts--</hi>Was it the owners only of the valuable property now lost to them that did this? Alas, no! For Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.37">Lu 8:37</reference>) says, "Then the whole multitude of the country of the Gadarenes round about besought Him to depart from them; for they were taken with great fear." The evil spirits had thus, alas! their object. Irritated, the people could not suffer His presence; yet awe-struck, they dared not order Him off: so they entreat Him to withdraw, and--He takes them at their word. <div eID="gen26832" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4290211445192524aa3d068a409877cb6ceb42d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13939"/><div sID="gen26833" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13939"/><hi type="bold">18. he that had been possessed with the devil prayed him that he might be with him--</hi>the grateful heart, fresh from the hand of demons, clinging to its wondrous Benefactor. How exquisitely natural! <div eID="gen26833" type="x-p"/>
entries.54aa7afe81da450e246b263b463cf6dc8ba041b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13940"/><div sID="gen26834" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13940"/><hi type="bold">19. Howbeit, Jesus suffered him not, &c.--</hi>To be a missionary for Christ, in the region where he was so well known and so long dreaded, was a far nobler calling than to follow Him where nobody had ever heard of him, and where other trophies not less illustrious could be raised by the same power and grace. <div eID="gen26834" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc4e7bfd96489e26d4fb226856913a73d0626f5f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13941"/><div sID="gen26835" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13941"/><hi type="bold">20. And he departed, and began to publish--</hi>not only among his friends, to whom Jesus immediately sent him, but<div eID="gen26835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26836" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Decapolis--</hi>so called, as being a region of ten cities. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.4.25">Mt 4:25</reference>).<div eID="gen26836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how great things Jesus had done for him: and all men did marvel--</hi>Throughout that considerable region did this monument of mercy proclaim his new-found Lord; and some, it is to be hoped, did more than "marvel."<div eID="gen26837" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.5.21-Mark.5.43">Mr 5:21-43</reference>. The Daughter of Jairus Raised to Life--The Woman with an Issue of Blood Healed. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.9.18-Matt.9.26">Mt 9:18-26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.8.41-Luke.8.56">Lu 8:41-56</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26838" type="x-p"/> The occasion of this scene will appear presently.<div eID="gen26838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26839" type="x-p"/> Jairus' Daughter (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.21-Mark.5.24">Mr 5:21-24</reference>). <div eID="gen26839" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3985e72fe2d7076a6ce5b36b85a03a07fb90396: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13942"/><div sID="gen26840" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13942"/><hi type="bold">21. And when Jesus was passed over again by ship unto the other side--</hi>from the Gadarene side of the lake, where He had parted with the healed demoniac, to the west side, at Capernaum.<div eID="gen26840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26841" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">much people gathered unto him--</hi>who "gladly received Him; for they were all waiting for Him" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.40">Lu 8:40</reference>). The abundant teaching earlier that day (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.1">Mr 4:1</reference>, &c., and <reference osisRef="Matt.13.1-Matt.13.58">Mt 13:1-58</reference>) had only whetted the people's appetite: and disappointed, as would seem, that He had left them in the evening to cross the lake, they remain hanging about the beach, having got a hint, probably through some of His disciples, that He would be back the same evening. Perhaps they witnessed at a distance the sudden calming of the tempest. The tide of our Lord's popularity was now fast rising.<div eID="gen26841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26842" type="x-p"/> and he was nigh unto the sea. <div eID="gen26842" type="x-p"/>
entries.18f2758969131722379a8cea4a215097398767a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13943"/><div sID="gen26843" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13943"/><hi type="bold">22. And, behold, there cometh one of the rulers of the synagogue--</hi>of which class there were but few who believed in Jesus (<reference osisRef="John.7.48">Joh 7:48</reference>). One would suppose from this that the ruler had been with the multitude on the shore, anxiously awaiting the return of Jesus, and immediately on His arrival had accosted Him as here related. But Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.18">Mt 9:18</reference>) tells us that the ruler came to Him while He was in the act of speaking at His own table on the subject of fasting; and as we must suppose that this converted publican ought to know what took place on that memorable occasion when he made a feast to his Lord, we conclude that here the right order is indicated by the First Evangelist alone.<div eID="gen26843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26844" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jairus by name--</hi>or "Jaeirus." It is the same name as Jair, in the Old Testament (<reference osisRef="Num.32.41">Nu 32:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.10.3">Jud 10:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.2.5">Es 2:5</reference>).<div eID="gen26844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and when he saw him, he fell at his feet--</hi>in Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.18">Mt 9:18</reference>), "worshipped Him." The meaning is the same in both. <div eID="gen26845" type="x-p"/>
entries.b64633226a963ac60d3ee95109b2dd25d002ea6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13944"/><div sID="gen26846" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13944"/><hi type="bold">23. And besought him greatly, saying, My little daughter--</hi>Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.42">Lu 8:42</reference>) says, "He had one only daughter, about twelve years of age." According to a well-known rabbin, quoted by Lightfoot, a daughter, till she had completed her twelfth year, was called "little," or "a little maid"; after that, "a young woman."<div eID="gen26846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lieth at the point of death--</hi>Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.18">Mt 9:18</reference>) gives it thus: "My daughter is even now dead"--"has just expired." The news of her death reached the father after the cure of the woman with the issue of blood: but Matthew's brief account gives only the result, as in the case of the centurion's servant (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.5">Mt 8:5</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen26847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26848" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come and lay thy hands on her, that she may be healed; and she shall live--</hi>or, "that she may be healed and live," according to a fully preferable reading. In one of the class to which this man belonged, so steeped in prejudice, such faith would imply more than in others.<div eID="gen26848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26849" type="x-p"/> The Woman with an Issue of Blood Healed (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.24-Mark.5.34">Mr 5:24-34</reference>). <div eID="gen26849" type="x-p"/>
entries.d20b77047c05ed96e2355585fdedffc8ae34999d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13945"/><div sID="gen26850" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13945"/><hi type="bold">24. And Jesus went with him; and much people followed him, and thronged him--</hi>The word in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.42">Lu 8:42</reference>) is stronger--"choked," "stifled Him." <div eID="gen26850" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a662f8534d7c06a75183cc7a8c0b76902ea8beb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13946"/><div sID="gen26851" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13946"/><hi type="bold">26. And had suffered many things of many physicians--</hi>The expression perhaps does not necessarily refer to the suffering she endured under medical treatment, but to the much varied treatment which she underwent.<div eID="gen26851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse--</hi>pitiable case, and affectingly aggravated; emblem of our natural state as fallen creatures (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.5">Eze 16:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.6">6</reference>), and illustrating the worse than vanity of all human remedies for spiritual maladies (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">Ho 5:13</reference>). The higher design of all our Lord's miracles of healing irresistibly suggests this way of viewing the present case, the propriety of which will still more appear as we proceed. <div eID="gen26852" type="x-p"/>
entries.82b39aa850925bf6291a61eb93f406c1e5fdc155: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13947"/><div sID="gen26853" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13947"/><hi type="bold">27. When she had heard of Jesus, came--</hi>This was the right experiment at last. What had she "heard of Jesus?" No doubt it was His marvellous cures she had heard of; and the hearing of these, in connection with her bitter experience of the vanity of applying to any other, had been blessed to the kindling in her soul of a firm confidence that He who had so willingly wrought such cures on others was able and would not refuse to heal her also.<div eID="gen26853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the press behind--</hi>shrinking, yet seeking.<div eID="gen26854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26855" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">touched his garment--</hi>According to the ceremonial law, the touch of anyone having the disease which this woman had would have defiled the person touched. Some think that the recollection of this may account for her stealthily approaching Him in the crowd behind, and touching but the hem of His garment. But there was an instinct in the faith which brought her to Jesus, which taught her, that if that touch could set her free from the defiling disease itself, it was impossible to communicate defilement to Him, and that this wondrous Healer must be above such laws. <div eID="gen26855" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d29779e0996d9dad925a5fe07cfc036b8e1d9cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13948"/><div sID="gen26856" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13948"/><hi type="bold">28. For she said--</hi>"within herself" (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.21">Mt 9:21</reference>).<div eID="gen26856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole--</hi>that is, if I may but come in contact with this glorious Healer at all. Remarkable faith this! <div eID="gen26857" type="x-p"/>
entries.1066e77e74ff6cbf07d5727664989f53d27305b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13949"/><div sID="gen26858" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13949"/><hi type="bold">29. And straightway the fountain of her blood was dried up--</hi>Not only was her issue of blood stanched (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.44">Lu 8:44</reference>), but the cause of it was thoroughly removed, insomuch that by her bodily sensations she immediately knew herself perfectly cured. <div eID="gen26858" type="x-p"/>
entries.786f7c818029e90c51a058c96fdefcb5e830e88a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13950"/><div sID="gen26859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13950"/><hi type="bold">30. And Jesus immediately knowing in himself that virtue--</hi>or "efficacy."<div eID="gen26859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">had gone out of him--</hi>He was conscious of the forthgoing of His healing power, which was not--as in prophets and apostles--something foreign to Himself and imparted merely, but what He had dwelling within Him as "His own fulness."<div eID="gen26860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turned him about in the press--</hi>crowd.<div eID="gen26861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26862" type="x-p"/> and said, Who touched my clothes? <div eID="gen26862" type="x-p"/>
entries.b48c98f0f3e7bd7688f5ce4ff236cad4a03d0537: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13951"/><div sID="gen26863" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13951"/><hi type="bold">31. And his disciples said unto him--</hi>Luke says (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.45">Lu 8:45</reference>), "When all denied, Peter and they that were with Him said, Master."<div eID="gen26863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou seest the multitude thronging thee, and sayest thou, Who touched me?--</hi>"Askest thou, Lord, who touched Thee? Rather ask who touched Thee not in such a throng." "And Jesus said, Somebody hath touched Me"--"a certain person has touched Me"--"for I perceive that virtue is gone out of Me" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.46">Lu 8:46</reference>). Yes, the multitude "thronged and pressed Him"--they jostled against Him, but all involuntarily; they were merely carried along; but one, one only--"a certain person--TOUCHED Him," with the conscious, voluntary, dependent touch of faith, reaching forth its hand expressly to have contact with Him. This and this only Jesus acknowledges and seeks out. Even so, as Augustine long ago said, multitudes still come similarly close to Christ in the means of grace, but all to no purpose, being only sucked into the crowd. The voluntary, living contact of faith is that electric conductor which alone draws virtue out of Him. <div eID="gen26864" type="x-p"/>
entries.478ab4cde912c0555c39a2955cba10fe7f649af9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13952"/><div sID="gen26865" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13952"/><hi type="bold">32. And he looked round about to see her that had done this thing--</hi>not for the purpose of summoning forth a culprit, but, as we shall presently see, to obtain from the healed one a testimony to what He had done for her. <div eID="gen26865" type="x-p"/>
entries.eec11e082366b5bf2cd883a7ee8725439c3988cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13953"/><div sID="gen26866" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13953"/><hi type="bold">33. But the woman, fearing and trembling, knowing what was done in her--</hi>alarmed, as a humble, shrinking female would naturally be, at the necessity of so public an exposure of herself, yet conscious that she had a tale to tell which would speak for her.<div eID="gen26866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26867" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth--</hi>In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.47">Lu 8:47</reference>) it is, "When the woman saw that she was not hid, she came trembling, and falling down before Him, she declared unto Him before all the people for what cause she had touched Him, and how she was healed immediately." This, though it tried the modesty of the believing woman, was just what Christ wanted in dragging her forth, her public testimony to the facts of her case--the disease, with her abortive efforts at a cure, and the instantaneous and perfect relief which her touching the Great Healer had brought her. <div eID="gen26867" type="x-p"/>
entries.b41ee270f1adbe24f41390d896bbfb2e7ac5fb41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13954"/><div sID="gen26868" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13954"/><hi type="bold">34. And he said unto her, Daughter--</hi>"be of good comfort" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.48">Lu 8:48</reference>).<div eID="gen26868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26869" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague--</hi>Though healed as soon as she believed, it seemed to her a stolen cure--she feared to acknowledge it. Jesus therefore sets His royal seal upon it. But what a glorious dismissal from the lips of Him who is "our Peace" is that, "Go in peace!"<div eID="gen26869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26870" type="x-p"/> Jairus' Daughter Raised to Life (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.35-Mark.5.43">Mr 5:35-43</reference>). <div eID="gen26870" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed083f8643b1d34f71605b5859b7315fecadad5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13955"/><div sID="gen26871" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13955"/><hi type="bold">35.
