Thy daughter is dead; why troublest thou the Master any further?--</hi>the Teacher. <div eID="gen26871" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e7ce1b06eb3255ea4d56ba8e5d06ee8813faeec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13956"/><div sID="gen26872" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13956"/><hi type="bold">36. he saith unto the ruler of the synagogue, Be not afraid, only believe--</hi>Jesus, knowing how the heart of the agonized father would sink at the tidings, and the reflections at the delay which would be apt to rise in his mind, hastens to reassure him, and in His accustomed style: <hi type="bold">"Be not afraid, only believe"--</hi>words of unchanging preciousness and power! How vividly do such incidents bring out Christ's knowledge of the human heart and tender sympathy! (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.15">He 4:15</reference>). <div eID="gen26872" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a2d801ab26294d34c3602d28b0d19d86efcffba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13957"/><div sID="gen26873" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13957"/><hi type="bold">37. And he suffered no man to follow him, save Peter, and James, and John the brother of James--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Mark.1.29">Mr 1:29</reference>). <div eID="gen26873" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f2f24afa65e4f14c1527d729aac1cb3c7fa45a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13958"/><div sID="gen26874" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13958"/><hi type="bold">38. And he cometh--</hi>rather, "they come."<div eID="gen26874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26875" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and seeth the tumult, and them that wept and wailed greatly--</hi>"the minstrels and the people making a noise" (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.23">Mt 9:23</reference>)--lamenting for the dead. (See <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.25">2Ch 35:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.20">Jr 9:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.16">Am 5:16</reference>). <div eID="gen26875" type="x-p"/>
entries.b996a913ca98924a7c67b7db289d2b812bc35e8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13959"/><div sID="gen26876" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13959"/><hi type="bold">39. And when he was come in, he saith unto them, Why make ye this ado, and weep? the damsel is not dead, but sleepeth--</hi>so brief her state of death as to be more like a short sleep. <div eID="gen26876" type="x-p"/>
entries.247030cccf519b9416bd4fd39a191c8cf93fa4d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13960"/><div sID="gen26877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13960"/><hi type="bold">40. And they laughed him to scorn--</hi>rather, simply, "laughed at Him"--"knowing that she was dead" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.53">Lu 8:53</reference>); an important testimony this to the reality of her death.<div eID="gen26877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">But when he had put them all out--</hi>The word is strong--"turned them all out"; meaning all those who were making this noise, and any others that may have been there from sympathy, that only those might be present who were most nearly concerned, and those whom He had Himself brought as witnesses of the great act about to be done.<div eID="gen26878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he taketh the father and the mother of the damsel, and them that were with him--</hi>Peter, and James, and John.<div eID="gen26879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26880" type="x-p"/> and entereth in where the damsel was lying. <div eID="gen26880" type="x-p"/>
entries.aeefc85c5a87d98ae61922eff920030dac8082be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13961"/><div sID="gen26881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13961"/><hi type="bold">41. And he took the damsel by the hand--</hi>as He did Peter's mother-in-law (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.31">Mr 1:31</reference>).<div eID="gen26881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and said unto her, Talitha cumi--</hi>The words are Aramaic, or Syro-Chaldaic, the then language of Palestine. Mark loves to give such wonderful words just as they were spoken. See <reference osisRef="Mark.7.34">Mr 7:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.14.36">14:36</reference>. <div eID="gen26882" type="x-p"/>
entries.d751984d0e85a93167cdfdbf4247452f6017e793: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13962"/><div sID="gen26883" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13962"/><hi type="bold">42. And straightway the damsel--</hi>The word here is different from that in <reference osisRef="Mark.5.39-Mark.5.41">Mr 5:39-41</reference>, and signifies "young maiden," or "little girl."<div eID="gen26883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26884" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">arose, and walked--</hi>a vivid touch evidently from an eye-witness.<div eID="gen26884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And they were astonished with a great astonishment--</hi>The language here is the strongest. <div eID="gen26885" type="x-p"/>
entries.398c2e884043608715cb8dd34f58ca450c1d5120: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13963"/><div sID="gen26886" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13963"/><hi type="bold">43. And he charged them straitly--</hi>strictly.<div eID="gen26886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26887" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that no man should know it--</hi>The only reason we can assign for this is His desire not to let the public feeling regarding Him come too precipitately to a crisis.<div eID="gen26887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and commanded that something should be given her to eat--</hi>in token of perfect restoration. <chapter eID="Mark.5"/>

entries.fe26ecedcaa908eecb8a46f1a91c8b1acfba88d9: <div eID="gen39260" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen39261" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39262" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39262" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39261" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39263" type="x-p"/> The man possessed with a legion of demons cured, vv. 1-20. He raises Jairus's daughter to life, and cures the woman who had an issue of blood, vv. 21-43. <div eID="gen39263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39264" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen39264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39265" type="x-p"/> The Gadarenes - Some of the MSS. have Gergasenes, and some of them Gerasenes. Griesbach seems to prefer the latter. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.8.28">Mat 8:28</reference>. <div eID="gen39265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39266" type="x-p"/> The Gadarenes were included within the limits of the Gergasenes. Dr. Lightfoot supposes that, of the two demoniacs mentioned here, one was of Gadara, and consequently a heathen, the other was a Gergesenian, and consequently a Jew; and he thinks that Mark and Luke mention the Gadarene demoniac because his case was a singular one, being the only heathen cured by our Lord, except the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman.
entries.d5128692efd3f8b980ea818e78beae5315b6e891: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen39266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39267" type="x-p"/> A man with an unclean spirit - There are two mentioned by Matthew, who are termed demoniacs. See on <reference osisRef="Mar.1.23">Mar 1:23</reference> (note).
entries.bf8af1b8659d2193717b6213d4c5200f9905198f: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen39267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39268" type="x-p"/> Who had his dwelling among the tombs - See <reference osisRef="Mat.8.28">Mat 8:28</reference>.
entries.a60b6adf5efe700805e55a8652f2de334a43c37a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen39268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39269" type="x-p"/> With fetters and chains - His strength, it appears was supernatural, no kind of chains being strong enough to confine him. With several, this man would have passed for an outrageous madman, and diabolic influence be entirely left out of the question; but it is the prerogative of the inspired penman only, to enter into the nature and causes of things; and how strange is it, that because men cannot see as far as the Spirit of God does, therefore they deny his testimony. "There was no devil; there can be none." Why? "Because we have never seen one, and we think the doctrine absurd." Excellent reason! And do you think that any man who conscientiously believes his Bible will give any credit to you? Men sent from God, to bear witness to the truth, tell us there were demoniacs in their time; you say, "No, they were only diseases." Whom shall we credit? The men sent from God, or you?
entries.7951675278bd117252e45f91128fd1e777cfa2c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen39269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39270" type="x-p"/> Crying and cutting himself with stones - In this person's case we see a specimen of what Satan could do in all the wicked, if God should permit him; but even the devil himself has his chain; and he who often binds others, is always bound himself.
entries.9f977014be69ca68c4d78b9d717da1b5c96fcb5c: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen39270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39271" type="x-p"/> Worshipped him - Did him homage; compelled thereto by the power of God. How humiliating to Satan, thus to be obliged to acknowledge the superiority of Christ!
entries.3b825f9b812c40e81c1ed3ad147511177830a8df: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen39271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39272" type="x-p"/> What have I to do with thee - Or, What is it to thee and me, or why dost thou trouble thyself with me? See on <reference osisRef="Mar.1.24">Mar 1:24</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Mat.8.29">Mat 8:29</reference> (note), where the idiom and meaning are explained. <div eID="gen39272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39273" type="x-p"/> Jesus - This is omitted by four MSS., and by several in <reference osisRef="Luk.8.28">Luk 8:28</reference>, and by many of the first authority in <reference osisRef="Mat.8.29">Mat 8:29</reference> (note). See the note on this latter place.
entries.9c1f4e070bc65d466eaa20f329180cd4f586c63e: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen39273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39274" type="x-p"/> Legion: for we are many - Could a disease have spoken so? "No, there was no devil in the case; the man spoke according to the prejudice of his countrymen." And do you think that the Spirit of God could employ himself in retailing such ridiculous and nonsensical prejudices? "But the evangelist gives these as this madman's words, and it was necessary that, as a faithful historian, he should mention these circumstances." But this objection is destroyed by the parallel place in Luke, <reference osisRef="Luk.8.30">Luk 8:30</reference>, where the inspired writer himself observes, that the demoniac was called Legion, because many demons had entered into him.
entries.837b9b52b920129e4c19518c907798ce6f075f67: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen39274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39275" type="x-p"/> Out of the country - Strange that these accursed spirits should find it any mitigation of their misery to be permitted to exercise their malevolence in a particular district! But as this is supposed to have been a heathen district, therefore the demons might consider themselves in their own territories; and probably they could act there with less restraint than they could do in a country where the worship of God was established. See on <reference osisRef="Mar.5.1">Mar 5:1</reference> (note).
entries.f8d3168e92ca50bc9fb2a232c751581bc63102a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen39275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39276" type="x-p"/> A great herd of swine - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.8.30">Mat 8:30</reference>.
entries.abb5c4458b917b0e98f5df3857a859bc318116c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen39276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39277" type="x-p"/> All the devils - Παντες, all, is omitted by many MSS. and versions; Griesbach leaves it out of the text. Οἱ δαιμονες is omitted also by several: Griesbach leaves it doubtful. Probably it should be read thus, And they besought him, saying.
entries.4e30776aa89601a2bafff89c3c2d2e1cfcfcdd72: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen39277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39278" type="x-p"/> Gave them leave - For επετρεψεν, DH, three others, and three copies of the Itala have επεμψεν, sent them.
entries.b9408cea8047e584f739ecc7bd19fee6e7e85a7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen39278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39279" type="x-p"/> The swine - Instead of τους χοιρους, BCDL, three others, Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, Vulgate, and Itala, read αυτους, them - And they that fed Them fled. Griesbach has adopted this reading.
entries.9a90cac0d79ab111135502d05399707045c920e5: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen39279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39280" type="x-p"/> That - had the legion - This is omitted by D, and two others, Ethiopic, Persic, Vulgate, and all the Itala but one. Mill, Bengel, and Griesbach, think it should be omitted.
entries.1b271e0359499e125fd8899be61d9806bfca25d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen39280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39281" type="x-p"/> Suffered him not - Ὁ δε Ιησους, Howbeit Jesus, is omitted by ABKLM, twenty-seven others, both the Syriac, both the Persic, Coptic, Gothic, Vulgate, and one of the Itala. Mill and Bengel approve of the omission, and Griesbach leaves it out of the text. <div eID="gen39281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39282" type="x-p"/> Go home to thy friends, etc. - This was the cause why Jesus would not permit him to follow him now, because he would not have the happiness of his relatives deferred, who must exceedingly rejoice at seeing the wonders which the Lord had wrought.
entries.7149f85f126c65b911538270bd7bbe8478e8e317: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen39282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39283" type="x-p"/> Decapolis - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.4.25">Mat 4:25</reference> (note).
entries.f7fd928c7da82b1f45426a2bee0d927d78de50f8: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen39283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39284" type="x-p"/> My little daughter - Το θυγατριον μου, that little daughter of mine. The words express much tenderness and concern. Luke observes, <reference osisRef="Luk.8.42">Luk 8:42</reference>, that she was his only daughter, and was about twelve years of age. <div eID="gen39284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39285" type="x-p"/> At the point of death - Εσχατως εχει, in the last extremity, the last gasp. <div eID="gen39285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39286" type="x-p"/> See on <reference osisRef="Mat.9.18">Mat 9:18</reference> (note).
entries.d81cd3dbcc6b066554595e467ab2662ed01d0c3c: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen39286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39287" type="x-p"/> A certain woman - See <reference osisRef="Mat.9.20">Mat 9:20</reference>.
entries.8b6cd00036baab009b8cf460c4062b4d42562f88: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen39287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39288" type="x-p"/> Had suffered many things of many physicians, - and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse - No person will wonder at this account, when he considers the therapeutics of the Jewish physicians in reference to hemorrhages, especially of the kind with which this woman was afflicted. <div eID="gen39288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39289" type="x-p"/> Rabbi Jochanan says: "Take of gum Alexandria, of alum, and of crocus hortensis, the weight of a zuzee each; let them be bruised together, and given in wine to the woman that hath an issue of blood. But if this fail, "Take of Persian onions nine logs, boil them in wine, and give it to her to drink: and say, Arise from thy flux. But should this fail, "Set her in a place where two ways meet, and let her hold a cup of wine in her hand; and let somebody come behind and affright her, and say, Arise from thy flux. But should this do no good, "Take a handful of cummin and a handful of crocus, and a handful of faenu-greek; let these be boiled, and given her to drink, and say, Arise from thy flux. But should this also fail, "Dig seven trenches, and burn in them some cuttings of vines not yet circumcised (vines not four years old); and let her take in her hand a cup of wine, and let her be led from this trench and set down over that, and let her be removed from that, and set down over another: and in each removal say unto her, Arise from thy flux." Dr. Lightfoot gives these as a sample, out of many others, extracted from Bab. Shabb. fol. 110. <div eID="gen39289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39290" type="x-p"/> And from some of these nostrums it is evident the woman could not be bettered, and from some others it is as evident that she must be made worse; and from all together it is indubitably certain that she must have suffered many things; - and from the persons employed, the expense of the medicaments, and the number of years she was afflicted, as she was not a person of great opulence, it is most perfectly credible that she spent all that she had. She was therefore a fit patient for the Great Physician. <div eID="gen39290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39291" type="x-p"/> The case of this woman was a very afflicting one: <div eID="gen39291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39292" type="x-p"/> 1. Because of the nature of her malady; it was such as could not be made public, without exposing her to shame and contempt. <div eID="gen39292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39293" type="x-p"/> 2. It was an inveterate disorder; it had lasted twelve years. <div eID="gen39293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39294" type="x-p"/> 3. It was continual; she appears to have had no interval of health. <div eID="gen39294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39295" type="x-p"/> 4. Her disorder was aggravated by the medicines she used - she suffered much, etc. <div eID="gen39295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39296" type="x-p"/> 5. Her malady was ruinous both to her health and circumstances - she spent all that she had. <div eID="gen39296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39297" type="x-p"/> 6. She was now brought to the last point of wretchedness, want, and despair; she was growing worse, and had neither money nor goods to make another experiment to procure her health. <div eID="gen39297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39298" type="x-p"/> 7. She was brought so low by her disorder as to be incapable of earning any thing to support her wretched life a little longer. <div eID="gen39298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39299" type="x-p"/> It has been said, and the saying is a good one, "Man's extremity is God's opportunity." Never could the power and goodness of God be shown in a more difficult and distressful case. And now Jesus comes, and she is healed.
entries.a32514e1a0dbffd4588cb08b981abad9605693b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen39299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39300" type="x-p"/> Came in the press behind - She had formed her resolution in faith, she executes it, notwithstanding her weakness, etc., with courage; and now she finds it crowned with success.
entries.d89c4bfac934f557172395f36125ead87431d6a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen39300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39301" type="x-p"/> Thou seest the multitude thronging then, etc. - Many touch Jesus who are not healed by him: the reason is, they do it not by faith, through a sense of their wants, and a conviction of his ability and willingness to save them. Faith conveys the virtue of Christ into the soul, and spiritual health is the immediate consequence of this received virtue.
entries.cff7dc6a1867f43deb9c33f9ec6a94734208b858: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen39301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39302" type="x-p"/> Fearing and trembling - See <reference osisRef="Mat.9.22">Mat 9:22</reference>.
entries.1b5b511d4f75d5c0c660cf0ac8ec16509e9f4035: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen39302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39303" type="x-p"/> Be whole of thy plague - Rather, continue whole, not, be whole, for she was already healed: but this contains a promise, necessary to her encouragement, that her disorder should afflict her no more.
entries.0670dc4986983cc07cd375188092dd1d949a9f7f: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen39303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39304" type="x-p"/> Why troublest thou the Master - These people seem to have had no other notion of our Lord than that of an eminent physician, who might be useful while there was life, but afterwards could do nothing.
entries.38233cfdccf41a63f9314735e01061b1cbad785a: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen39304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39305" type="x-p"/> Jesus - saith - These words were spoken by our Lord to the afflicted father, immediately on his hearing of the death of his child, to prevent that distress which he otherwise must have felt on finding that the case was now, humanly speaking, hopeless.
entries.1e9e8ee2ead15d924c8a6d73bdd2dc069ae03057: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen39305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39306" type="x-p"/> He cometh - But ερχονται, they come, is the reading of ABCDF, four others, and several versions. <div eID="gen39306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39307" type="x-p"/> Wept and wailed - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.9.23">Mat 9:23</reference> (note).
entries.212c63367310e66341cb33be0ab9cbf5aeb24b20: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen39307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39308" type="x-p"/> The father and the mother - Prudence required that they should be present, and be witnesses of the miracle. <div eID="gen39308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39309" type="x-p"/> And them that were with him - That is, Peter, James, and John, <reference osisRef="Mar.5.37">Mar 5:37</reference>. It is remarkable that our Lord gave a particular preference to these three disciples, beyond all the rest, on three very important occasions: <div eID="gen39309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39310" type="x-p"/> 1. They were present at the transfiguration. <div eID="gen39310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39311" type="x-p"/> 2. At the raising of Jairus's daughter. <div eID="gen39311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39312" type="x-p"/> 3. At his agony in the garden of Gethsemane. <div eID="gen39312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39313" type="x-p"/> Where the damsel was lying - Ανακειμενον, lying. This word is very doubtful. BDL, one other, Coptic, and later Arabic, with five of the Itala, omit it. Other MSS. express the same idea in five different words: Griesbach leaves it out of the text. See his Testament.
entries.9697fb676f4472442543fb089d2bd051912d712f: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen39313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39314" type="x-p"/> Talitha cumi - , This is mere Syriac, the proper translation of which the evangelist has given. The Codex Bezae has a very odd and unaccountable reading here, ῥαββι. θαβιτα κουμι, My master. Damsel arise. Suidas quotes this place under the word Αββακουμ thus ταληθα κουμ. Κουμ is the reading of several ancient MSS., but it is certainly a faulty one.
entries.509859b95ecfba8478253cf7ae52e26ae0930876: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen39314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39315" type="x-p"/> Something should be given her to eat - For though he had employed an extraordinary power to bring her to life, he wills that she should be continued in existence by the use of ordinary means. The advice of the heathen is a good one: - <div eID="gen39315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39316" type="x-p"/> Nec Deus intersit, nisi dignus vindice nodus Inciderit. <div eID="gen39316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39317" type="x-p"/> Horat "When the miraculous power of God is necessary, let it be resorted to: when it is not necessary, let the ordinary means be used." <div eID="gen39317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39318" type="x-p"/> To act otherwise would be to tempt God. <div eID="gen39318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39319" type="x-p"/> While Christ teaches men the knowledge of the true God, and the way of salvation, he at the same time teaches them lessons of prudence, economy, and common sense. And it is worthy of remark, that all who are taught of him are not only saved, but their understandings are much improved. True religion, civilization, mental improvement, common sense, and orderly behavior, go hand in hand.  <chapter eID="Mark.5"/> <div eID="gen39319" type="x-p"/>

Verse 15. Sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind. There could be no doubt of the reality of this miracle. The man had been well known. He had long dwelt among the tombs, an object of terror and alarm. To see him all at once peaceful, and calm, and rational, was proof that it was the power of God only that had done it.

They were afraid. They were awed, as in the presence of God. The word does not mean here that they feared that any evil would happen to them, but that they were affected with awe; they felt that God was there; they were struck with astonishment at what Jesus had done.

entries.e40d7e1476e45753983f426a02d2e7fdec82204b:
Verse 19. Jesus suffered him not. Various reasons have been conjectured why Jesus did not suffer this malt to go with him. It might be, that he wished to leave him among the people, as a conclusive evidence of his power to work miracles. It might be that the man feared that if Jesus left him the devils would return, and that Jesus told him to remain to show to him that the cure was complete and that he had power over the devils when absent, as well as when present. But the probable reason is, that he desired to restore him to his family and friends. He was probably a man of influence, and Jesus was unwilling to delay the joy of his friends, and prolong their anxiety, by suffering him to remain away from them.

entries.58cbe4d2cdc0c815e35be8cbb0606d2c9fdbe1ec: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.5.3" sID="gen98089" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.5.3">Mark 5:3</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And no man could bind him, not even with chains</hi> Naturally, he was not able to break the chains; and hence we infer that Satan is sometimes permitted to make extraordinary movements, the effect of which goes beyond our comprehension and beyond ordinary means. We often perceive in madmen much greater strength than belongs to their natural capacity; and we are not at liberty to deny that, in such cases, the devil does his part when God permits him: but the force, which is described by the Evangelists, was far greater. <note n="548"> <div sID="gen98091" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais l'effort et la violence que les Evangelistes deserlvent estoit bien autre et plus grande</foreign>;” — “but the effort and the violence, which the Evangelists describe, was quite different and much greater.”<div eID="gen98091" type="x-p"/> </note> It was indeed a sad and shocking exhibition, but may serve to remind us how wretched and alarming it is to be placed under the tyranny of Satan, and also that bodily agony, however violent or cruel, is not more to be dreaded than distress of mind.<div eID="gen98090" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98089" osisID="Mark.5.3" type="section"/>
entries.3d4b6ff26721831d3d54e93965e3f89e0aa97d21: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.5.6" sID="gen98092" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.5.6">Mark 5:6</reference></hi> <hi type="italic">Worshipped him</hi> <note n="549"> <div sID="gen98094" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">S'enclina devant luy</foreign>;” — “kneeled down before him.”<div eID="gen98094" type="x-p"/> </note> The arrangement of the narrative may be thus stated. When the demoniacs came to meet him, Christ ordered <hi type="italic">the unclean spirits to go out of them, </hi>and then they prayed and entreated that he would not <hi type="italic">torment them before the time</hi> <hi type="italic"> </hi>The <hi type="italic">worship, </hi>therefore, did not precede Christ’s words: nor did they complain that Christ gave them uneasiness, <note n="550"> <div sID="gen98095" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et ils ne se sont point plainds que Christ les tormentast, sinon quand il les pressoit de sortir</foreign>;” — “and they did not complain that Christ tormented them, till he urged them to go out.”<div eID="gen98095" type="x-p"/> </note> till he urged them to go out. We ought to be aware that they did not come of their own accord into the presence of Christ, but were drawn by a secret exercise of his authority. As they had formerly been accustomed to carry men off, in furious violence, to <hi type="italic">the tombs, </hi>so now a superior power compels them to appear reluctantly at the tribunal of their judge.<div eID="gen98093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98096" type="x-p"/>Hence we infer, that the whole of Satan’s kingdom is subject to the authority of Christ. <note n="551"> <div sID="gen98097" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que tout le regne de Satan est tenu en bride sous la domination de Christ</foreign>;” — “that all the kingdom of Satan is kept in check under the government of Christ.”<div eID="gen98097" type="x-p"/> </note> For the devils, when Christ summons them to appear before him, are not more at their own disposal than were the wretched men whom their tyranny was wont to drive about in every direction. At length, by the secret power of Christ, they are dragged before him, that, by casting them out, he may prove himself to be the deliverer of men. Reluctantly too they <hi type="italic">worship</hi> him, and their rebellious complaints testify that their confession was not made from choice, but was drawn from them by force.<div eID="gen98096" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98092" osisID="Mark.5.6" type="section"/>
entries.9139a64dec04a958a4798541ba8fa33f185530ed: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.5.9" sID="gen98105" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.5.9">Mark 5:9</reference></hi> <hi type="italic">My name is Legion.</hi> The devil was compelled by Christ to pronounce this word, that he might more fully display the greatness and excellence of his grace. There must have been good reasons why this man should have endured so severe a punishment as to have an army of devils, so to speak, dwelling within him. What compassion then was it, to rescue from so many deaths a man who was more than a thousand times ruined! It was a magnificent display of the power of Christ., that by his voice not one devil, but a great multitude of devils, were suddenly driven out. <hi type="italic">Legion</hi> denotes here not a definite number of men, but merely a great multitude.<div eID="gen98106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98107" type="x-p"/>Hence it is evident what a wretched creature man is, when he is deprived of the divine protection. Every man is not only exposed to a single devil, but becomes the retreat of vast numbers. This passage refutes also the common error, which has been borrowed by Jews and Christians from the heathens, that every man is attacked by his own particular devil? On the contrary, Scripture plainly declares, that, just as it pleases God, one devil <note n="554"> <div sID="gen98108" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">A scavoir que chacun hornroe ha son diable et son mauvals ange qui lui fait la guerre</foreign>;” — “namely, that each man has his devil and his evil angel who makes war with him.”<div eID="gen98108" type="x-p"/> </note> is sometimes sent to punish a whole nation, and at other times many devils are permitted to punish one man: as, on the other hand, one angel sometimes protects a whole nation, and every man has many angels to act as his guardians. There is the greater necessity for keeping diligent watch, lest so great a multitude of enemies should take us by surprise.<div eID="gen98107" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98105" osisID="Mark.5.9" type="section"/>
entries.64cf74c4fdc46dc64b1d9de32a34340eb980a487: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.5.10" sID="gen98109" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.5.10">Mark 5:10</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And entreated him earnestly</hi> Luke says, they requested that they might not be sent <hi type="italic">into the deep</hi> <hi type="italic"> </hi>Some explain these words to mean that they wished to avoid uninhabited places. <note n="555"> <div sID="gen98111" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ce qu'aucuns exposent comme si les diables n'eussent point voulu aller en lieu desert</foreign>;” — “which some explain as if the devils did not wish to go into a desert place.”<div eID="gen98111" type="x-p"/> </note> I rather view it as referring to their rage for doing mischief. As the devils have no other object than to prowl among men, like lions in search of prey, they are grieved at being plunged into the deep, where they will have no opportunity of injuring and ruining men. That this is the true meaning may be inferred from the words of Mark, who says that they requested that they might not be compelled to go <hi type="italic">out of the country</hi> In a word, they manifest their disposition to be such, that there is nothing which they more eagerly desire than the destruction of mankind.<div eID="gen98110" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98109" osisID="Mark.5.10" type="section"/>
entries.91fce56441b7ce94f2233535444ec97860fe197e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.5.15" sID="gen98114" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.5.15">Mark 5:15</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And they come to Jesus</hi> We have here a striking proof that not all who perceive the hand of God profit as they ought to do by yielding themselves to him in sincere godliness. Having seen the miracle, the Gadarenes were afraid, because the majesty of God shone brightly in Christ. So far they did right but now that they send him out of their territories, what could have been done worse than this? They too were scattered, and here is a shepherd to collect them or rather, it is God who stretches out his arms, through his Son, to embrace and carry to heaven those who were overwhelmed by the darkness of death. They choose rather to be deprived of the salvation which is offered to them, than to endure any longer the presence of Christ.<div eID="gen98115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98116" type="x-p"/>The apparent ground of their offense is the loss of the swine, but Luke assigns a loftier cause, that they were <hi type="italic">seized with a great fear</hi>; <note n="556"> <div sID="gen98117" type="x-p"/> “ ᾿Εφοβήθησαν, <hi type="italic">they were afraid, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.5.15">Mark 5:15</reference>,) is by most Commentators understood of <hi type="italic">fear </hi>lest they might suffer a yet greater calamity; but it rather denotes awe at the stupendous <hi type="italic">miracle</hi>.” —<hi type="italic"> Bloomfield</hi><div eID="gen98117" type="x-p"/> </note> and certainly, if they had been exasperated by the loss which they sustained, they would not have <hi type="italic">requested </hi>him, but would rudely have driven him out. They honor him as God’s minister, and yet are so struck with dread as to desire that he will go to a distance from them. Thus we see that they were not at all moved by a sense of the divine grace. And indeed, though all wicked men adore God, and bestow great pains on appeasing him, yet if they had their choice, they would withdraw to the greatest possible distance from him: for his face is terrible, so long as they contemplate him as a Judge, and not as a Father. The consequence is, that the gospel, which is more delightful than any thing that can be conceived, is everywhere considered to be so dismal and severe, that a good part of the world would wish that it were buried.<div eID="gen98116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98118" type="x-p"/>And yet it is true that their fear was partly occasioned by their loss. Thus at the present day, so long as men believe that the kingdom of God is opposed to their interest, either of a public or private nature, they are prepossessed by a depraved and carnal fear, and have no relish for his grace. Accordingly, when he comes, they think that God does not regard them with favor, but rather with anger, and, so far as lies in their power, they send him to another place. It is a mark of shameful insensibility in those men, that the loss of their swine gives them more alarm than the salvation of their soul would give them joy.<div eID="gen98118" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98114" osisID="Mark.5.15" type="section"/>

Mark 5:34. Go in peace, and be delivered from thy scourge. From this exhortation we infer that the benefit which she had obtained was fully ratified, when she heard from the lips of Christ what she had already learned from experience: for we do not truly, or with a safe conscience, enjoy God’s benefits in any other way than by possessing them as contained in the treasury of his promises.
MATTHEW 9:23-26; MARK 5:35-43; LUKE 8:49-56
Matthew 9:23-26
Mark 5:35-43
Luke 8:49-56
23. And when Jesus came into the house of the ruler, and saw the musicians and the multitude making a noise, 24. He saith to them, Withdraw: for the young woman is not dead, but sleepeth: and they ridiculed him. 25. And when the multitude was put out, he entered and took hold of her hand, and the girl arose. 26. And this report spread into all that country.
35. While he is still speaking, there come from the ruler of the synagogue persons who say, Thy daughter is dead: why dost thou trouble the Master any farther? 36. And immediately on hearing the word which was said, he saith to the ruler of the synagogue, Fear not, only believe. 37. And he did not permit any one to follow him, except Peter, and James, and John the brother of James. 38. And he came into the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and saw the tumult, and persons who wept and lamented much. 39. And he entered, and said to them, Why do you vex yourselves and lament? the girl is not dead, but sleepeth. 40. And they ridiculed him. But, having put them all out, he taketh the father and mother of the girl, and those who were with him, and entereth where the girl is lying. 41. And he took hold of the hand of the girl, and said to her, Talitha-cumi: which is, if one interpret it, Girl, I say to thee, Arise. 42. And immediately the girl arose, and walked: for she was twelve years of age. And they were astonished with a great astonishment. 43. And he charged them earnestly, that no man should know it: and commanded them to give her something to eat.
49. While he was still speaking, one came from the house of the ruler of the synagogue, saying to him, Thy daughter is dead, do not trouble the Master. 50. But Jesus, having heard this, replied to the ruler, saying, Fear not, only believe, and she shall be cured. 51. And when he came into the house, he did not permit any one to enter, except Peter, and James, and John, and the father and mother of the girl. 52. And all were weeping and bewailing her. But he said, Weep not: she is not dead, but sleepeth. 53. And they ridiculed him, knowing that she was dead. 54. And he having put them all out, took hold of her hand, and cried out, saying, Girl, arise. 55. And her spirit returned, and she immediately arose: and he commanded to give her something to eat. 56. And her parents were astonished: but he charged them to tell no man what had been done.
entries.fb3df241054ab4697dc08c6740c0b996d3240b87: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.36" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.5.36" sID="gen97988" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.5.36">Mark 5:36</reference>. </hi><hi type="italic">Fear not, only believe.</hi> The message about her death had induced despair: for he had asked nothing from Christ but relief to the diseased young woman. Christ therefore bids him take care lest, by fear or distrust, he shut out that grace, to which death will be no hindrance. By this expression, <hi type="italic">only believe, </hi>he means that he will not want power, provided Jairus will allow him; and, at the same time, exhorts him to enlarge his heart with confidence, because there is no room to fear that his faith will be more extensive than the boundless power of God. And truly this is the case with us all: for God would be much more liberal in his communications to us, if we were not so close; but our own scanty desires hinder him from pouring out his gifts upon us in greater abundance. <note n="528"> <div sID="gen97990" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais la petitesse, et (par maniere de dire) la chicete de nostre foy, l'empesche de faire decouler plus abondamment ses biens sur nous</foreign>;” — “But the smallness and (so to speak) the niggardliness of our faith, hinders him from making his benefits flow more abundantly on us.”<div eID="gen97990" type="x-p"/> </note> In general, we are taught by this passage, that we cannot go beyond bounds in believing: because our faith, however large, will never embrace the hundredth part of the divine goodness.<div eID="gen97989" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.36" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97988" osisID="Mark.5.36" type="section"/>
entries.89b098a65c0e3f32b981ec518f18a138fa6e4567: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.37" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.5.37" sID="gen97991" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97992" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">37. </hi><hi type="italic">And did not permit any one to follow him.</hi> He forbade that they should be allowed to enter, either because they were unworthy to be his witnesses of the miracle, or because he did not choose that the miracle should be overpowered by a noisy crowd around him. It was better that the young woman, whose dead body they had beheld, should suddenly go out before the eyes of men, alive and full of rigor. <hi type="italic">Mark</hi> and <hi type="italic">Luke</hi> tell us that not more than three of the disciples were admitted, and both mention also the parents. <hi type="italic">Mark</hi> alone states that those who had accompanied Jairus when he came to supplicate Christ were admitted. Matthew, who is more concise, takes no notice of this circumstance.<div eID="gen97992" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.37" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97991" osisID="Mark.5.37" type="section"/>
entries.d6374d0a83705660d32ecaf2ade9bd94e8675e80: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.39" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.5.39" sID="gen97996" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.5.39">Mark 5:39</reference></hi> <hi type="italic">The girl sleepeth. Sleep </hi>is everywhere in Scripture employed to denote <hi type="italic">death; </hi>and there is no doubt but this comparison, taken from temporal rest, points out a future resurrection. But here Christ expressly makes a distinction between <hi type="italic">sleep </hi>and <hi type="italic">death, </hi>so as to excite an expectation of life. His meaning is, “You will presently see her raised up whom you suppose to be dead.” That he was <hi type="italic">ridiculed </hi>by thoughtless and ignorant people, who were wholly engrossed with profane lamentation, and who did not comprehend his design, ought not to awaken surprise. And yet this very circumstance was an additional confirmation of the miracle, that those persons entertained no doubt whatever as to her death.<div eID="gen97997" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.39" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97996" osisID="Mark.5.39" type="section"/>
entries.0a6df1130f219b725146073e210645c24ec89bf0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.41" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.5.41" sID="gen97998" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">41. </hi><hi type="italic">And he took hold of her hand, and said to her</hi> <hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.8.54">Luke 8:54</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And he took hold of her hand, and cried</hi> <hi type="italic"> </hi>Though naturally this <hi type="italic">cry </hi>was of no avail for recalling the senses of the deceased young woman, yet Christ intended to give a magnificent display of the power of his voice, that he might more fully accustom men to listen to his doctrine. It is easy to learn from this the great efficacy of the voice of Christ, which reaches even to the dead, and exerts a quickening influence on death itself. Accordingly, Luke says that <hi type="italic">her spirit returned, </hi>or, in other words, that immediately on being called, it obeyed the command of Christ.<div eID="gen97999" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.5.41" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97998" osisID="Mark.5.41" type="section"/>

43. And he charged them Though Christ did not admit all indiscriminately to behold this resurrection, yet the miracle might not have remained long concealed. And it would indeed have been improper to suppress that power of God, by which the whole world ought to be prepared for life. Why then does he enjoin silence on the young woman’s parents? Perhaps it was not so much about the fact itself, as about the manner of it, that he wished them to be silent, and that only for a time; for we see that there were other instances in which he sought out a proper occasion. Those who think that they were forbidden to speak for the purpose of whetting their desire, resort to a solution which is unnatural. I do acknowledge that Christ did not perform this miracle without the intention of making it known, but perhaps at a more fitting time, or after the dismission of a crowd among whom there was no prudence or moderation. He therefore intended to allow some delay, that they might in quietness and composure revolve the work of God.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="5" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. V.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 AND they <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 8 26.</ns0:note> came over unto the other side of the Sea, into the country of the Ga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />darenes.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And when he was come out of the ship, imme<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diately there met him out of the tombs, a man with an unclean spirit.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Who had <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> dwelling amongst the tombs, and no man could bind him, no not with chains.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Because that he had bin often bound, with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces, nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther could any man tame him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 And always night and day he was in the mountains, and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 But when he saw Jesus afar off, he ran and wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shipped him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 And cryed with a loud voice, and said, What have I to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of the most high God? I adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 (For he said unto him, Come out of the man, thou unclean spirit.)</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And he asked him, What <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy name? And he answered, saying, My name <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> Legion, for we are many.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 And he besought him much, that he would not send them away out of the country.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Now there was there nigh unto the mountains, a great herd of swine feeding.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And all the devils besought him, saying, Send us into the swine, that we may enter into them.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And forthwith Jesus gave them leave, And the unclean spirits went out, and entred into the swine, and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand) and were choaked in the Sea.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And they that fed the swine fled, and told <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> in the city, and in the country. And they went out to see what it was that was done.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting and cloathed, and in his right mind, and they were afraid.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 And they that saw <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> told them how it befel him that was possessed with the devil, and also con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning he swine.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">So Acts 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 39.</ns0:note> they began to pray him to depart out of their Coasts.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 And when he was come into the ship, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 8.3<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> he that had been possessed with the devil, prayed him that he might be with him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 Howbeit, Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him. Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 And he departed, and began to publish in De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />capolis how great things Jesus had done for him, And all men did marvel.<ns0:note place="bottom">This Famous piece of History hath the testimony of three Evangelists <ns0:hi>Matthew, Mark,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke.</ns0:hi> We meeting with it in <ns0:hi>Matthew,</ns0:hi> did not only largely open what passages <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> hath about it, but what both <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> have. See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 8.28, 29, 30. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> We shall only annex here some short notes. Interpreters judge the <ns0:hi>country</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Gergasenes,</ns0:hi> and of the <ns0:hi>Gaderenes</ns0:hi> mentioned here to have been the same, sometimes receiving the denomination from <ns0:hi>one City,</ns0:hi> sometimes from <ns0:hi>another</ns0:hi> in it. Why the Devils are called <ns0:hi>Vnclean Spirits,</ns0:hi> in Opposition to the Holy Spirit, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> We have formerly shewed, as also <ns0:hi>Why,</ns0:hi> they delight to be about <ns0:hi>Tombs,</ns0:hi> we have also shewed his Power, which (by Gods permission) he excerciseth upon Men, some he <ns0:hi>possesseth,</ns0:hi> and acteth the part of the Soul in them, (espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially as to the <ns0:hi>locomotive faculty</ns0:hi>) these are properly called <ns0:hi>Demo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />niacks,</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, others he <ns0:hi>afflicteth</ns0:hi> more as a Forreign agent, offering violence to them. Others he more secretly influenceth, by <ns0:hi>Impressions,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Suggestions,</ns0:hi> thus he still <ns0:hi>ordinarily worketh in the Children of disobedience, Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.2. nor are the People of God free from this <ns0:hi>impetus,</ns0:hi> tho being succoured by Christ, they are not so ordinarily overcome. Of the mighty Power of the Evil Angels to break Chains and Fetters, we need not doubt, considering that tho fallen from their first righteousness, they yet have their natural Power as Spirits. <ns0:hi>I adjure thee by God,</ns0:hi> is no more then, <ns0:hi>I solemnly intreat thee,</ns0:hi> it hath not the force of, <ns0:hi>Swear unto me by God,</ns0:hi> (as some would have it.) <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> mentioneth two of these <ns0:hi>Demoniaks, Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> but one; there were doubtless two, but probably one of them was not so raging as the others and therefore less taken notice of. Some think one of these Men, was an <ns0:hi>Heathen,</ns0:hi> the other a <ns0:hi>Iew.</ns0:hi> Because the term <ns0:hi>Legion</ns0:hi> which the <ns0:hi>Demoniack</ns0:hi> gives himself is an <ns0:hi>Heathen term,</ns0:hi> signifying a Squadron of Soldiers, about six thousand or more, as some reckon. 2. <ns0:hi>Christ was now in a Country full of Heathens.</ns0:hi> 3. The Woman of whose cure we next read was a <ns0:hi>Syrophenician.</ns0:hi> It is observable that a multitude of evil Spirits, is called by the name of <ns0:hi>the De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vil</ns0:hi>; because tho considered as individual Spirits they are many, yet in their Malice and mischievous designs against mankind, they are as one. O that the People of God were as well united in designs for his Glory! Some Interpreters start a Question here, not ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry easie to be resolved, <ns0:hi>viz. What made the Devils so desirous that Christ would not send them out of the Country.</ns0:hi> Their Answer is not improbable. That it was a Paganish ignorant Sot<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tish place, Where usually the Devil hath the best Markets, and the greatest Rule. For as it is said of Christ, that he could not do much in some places, where he came because of their <ns0:hi>unbelief:</ns0:hi> So neither can the Devil do much in some places, because of the <ns0:hi>Faith of the Gospel</ns0:hi> received by them. Hence it is observable, That as the Devil is not able to play his Game in any place amongst Christians, as he doth this Day amongst Heathens: So he hath much less Power at this day in places, where the Word of God is more generally known, and more faithfully Preached, than in o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther places where People are more Ignorant of the Scriptures, and have less faithful and frequent Preaching. In the latter he dealeth most by more inward Suggestions and Impressions. Our Learn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed Dr. <ns0:hi>Lightfoot</ns0:hi> observes it probable, that this City or Country was generally made up of <ns0:hi>Pagans,</ns0:hi> or Apostatized Jews, because they nourished so many <ns0:hi>Swine,</ns0:hi> which to the Jews were unclean Beasts. For other things relating to the Explication of this Histo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry, see the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 8.24, 25, 26.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:281" />21 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 9.1.</ns0:note> And when Jesus was passed over again by ship unto the other side, much people gathered to him and he was nigh unto the sea.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 8.41.</ns0:note> behold there cometh one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name and when he saw him, he fell at his feet.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 And besought him greatly, saying, My little daughter lyeth at the point of death, <ns0:hi>I pray thee</ns0:hi> come, and lay thy hands on her, that she may be healed, and she shall live.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 And <ns0:hi>Iesus</ns0:hi> went with him, and much people followed him, and thronged him.<ns0:note place="bottom">This whole History also is recorded both by <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke,</ns0:hi> and we have already in our Notes, upon <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 9.18, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> fully o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pened the several Passages of it mentioned by all the Evangelists, to which we refer the <ns0:hi>Reader.</ns0:hi> Christ was now come over again in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> where tho the <ns0:hi>Temple</ns0:hi> was not, yet there were <ns0:hi>Syna<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gogues,</ns0:hi> where the People did ordinarily assemble to <ns0:hi>Worship God.</ns0:hi> Nor were they without order in these <ns0:hi>Synagogues,</ns0:hi> they had one whom they called the <ns0:hi>Ruler</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Synagogue,</ns0:hi> who directed, and ordered the Affairs of that particular <ns0:hi>Synagogue.</ns0:hi> It is more pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable, that <ns0:hi>Iairus</ns0:hi> (here mentioned) was in that Sense so called, than because he was one of the Court of twenty three which the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> are said to have had in every City.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 And a certain woman, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Lev. 15.25.</ns0:note> which had an issue of blood twelve years.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 And had suffered many things of many physici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ans, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 For she said, If I may touch but his cloths, I shall be whole.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And straightway the fountain of her blood was dryed up, and she felt in her body, that she was heal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed of that plague.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 And Jesus immediately knowing in himself that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 6.19.</ns0:note> vertue had gone out of him, turned him about in the press, and said, Who touched my cloths.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 And his disciples said unto him, Thou seest the multitude thronging thee, and sayest thou, Who touch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed me?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 And he looked round about, to see her that had done this thing.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 But the woman fearing, and trembling, know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing what was done in her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 And he said unto her, Daughter, thy faith hath made the whole,<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 10.52.</ns0:note> go in peace, and be whole of thy plague.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 9.18. upon this whole History; containing a passage which happened in the way betwixt the place, where our Saviour first heard of the Sickness of <ns0:hi>Iairus</ns0:hi> his Daugh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter and his House, whither our Saviour was now going; we shall in these Histories observe our Saviour propounding several Que<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stions to Persons, of the matter to which they related, he could not be presumed to be ignorant, being as to his Divine Nature Om<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />niscient, but he only propounded them for the bettering of the knowledge of those to whom or amongst whom he spake, that his <ns0:hi>Miracles</ns0:hi> might be more fully, and distinctly understood. So also he is said to have known many things (as here, <ns0:hi>that Vertue was gone out of him</ns0:hi>) which he only knew as he was God, and knew all things. It is also observable how Christ incourageth the first <ns0:hi>Rudiments</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>saving Faith</ns0:hi> in Christ. All that we read of this Woman, is, that she said, <ns0:hi>If I may but touch the Hem of his Garment, I shall be whole,</ns0:hi> this was much short of her owning and receiving him as her Lord, and Saviour. It amounted to no more, than a perswasion she had of his Divine Power, and good<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, and that with respect to the healing of a bodily Distemper, nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther doth it import her believing him to be the Eternal Son of God, but one to whom God had Communicated a power of healing; in this confidence she cometh unto him, and toucheth the Border of his Garment, she is presently healed, Christ saith, <ns0:hi>her Faith had made her whole.</ns0:hi>Christ measureth her Faith by the light and means she had received, and accordingly rewards it, and if the Notion be true, that where he healed the Body, he also healed the Soul, this was the beginning of a greater Faith in her.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 While he yet spake, there came from the ruler of the synagogues <ns0:hi>house, certain</ns0:hi> which said, Thy daughter is dead, Why troublest thou thy Master any further?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 As soon as Jesus had heard the word that was spoken, he saith unto the ruler of the synagogue, Be not afraid, only believe.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 And he suffered no man to follow him, save Pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter, and James, and John the brother of James.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 And he cometh to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and seeth the tumult, and them that wept and wailed greatly.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 And when he was come in, he saith unto them, Why make you this ado, and weep? the damsel is not dead, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 11.11.</ns0:note> but sleepeth.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 And they laughed him to scorn. But when he had put them all out, he taketh the father and mother of the damsel, and them that were with him, and entreth in, where the damsel was lying.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">41 And he took the damsel by the hand, and saith unto her, Talitha cumi, which is being interpreted Damsel, I say unto thee arise.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="42">42 And straightway the damsel arose, and walked, for she was <ns0:hi>of the age</ns0:hi> of twelve years: And they were astonished with a great astonishment.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="43">43 And he charged them straightly, that no man should know it: and commanded that something should be given her to eat.<ns0:note place="bottom">There is nothing in this History needeth further Notes for Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plication, than what we gave in the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> 9. to which I here refer the Reader. There is nothing more accounta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble in all the passages of our Saviours Life, recorded by the Evan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gelists. Then the Charges that he gave to several Persons heal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by him. <ns0:hi>That no man should know it.</ns0:hi> Especially if we con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sider, 1. <ns0:hi>That he did not charge all so,</ns0:hi> he bid the Person pos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sessed with the Devil, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 29. of this Chapter, <ns0:hi>go home to his Friends, and tell them how great things the Lord had done for him.</ns0:hi> 2. That he could not expect to be concealed, had they yielded obedience, for his Miracles were done openly, and it was not like that all would keep silence, nay he commanded <ns0:hi>the Le<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />per to go and shew himself to the Priests.</ns0:hi> 3. <ns0:hi>Few of those thus Charged, did keep silence.</ns0:hi> Nor do we ever find that Christ re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />flected blame on them, from which yet we cannot acquit them. But we must not think to understand the Reasons of all Christs Actions and Speeches, he had doubtless wise ends in doing it, tho we do not understand them.</ns0:note>
